stem: A 4-month-old term male infant presents to your rural emergency department in July with 3 days of coryza and 24 hours of worsening cough and feed refusal. He weighs 6 kg and is on nasal prong oxygen 1 L/min. Bedside nasopharyngeal aspirate is positive for RSV. There is no history of prematurity, congenital heart disease or immune compromise.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 168, RR 68, SpO2 89 percent on 1 L/min NP, temp 37.9 C
data_table.Examination: Head bobbing, moderate subcostal and intercostal recessions, widespread wheeze and fine crackles, capillary refill 2 seconds
data_table.Investigations: Bedside gas pH 7.34, pCO2 48 mmHg, lactate 1.4 mmol/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in oxygen delivery?

options.text: Commence heated humidified high flow nasal cannula at 2 L/kg/min via age-appropriate interface, titrating FiO2 to keep SpO2 92 to 96 percent
options.rationale: AU bronchiolitis pathways use HFNC at 2 L/kg/min for infants failing standard flow oxygen with recessions and desaturation, before CPAP or intubation. FiO2 is titrated to a target SpO2 of 92 to 96 percent.

options.text: Continue nasal prong oxygen at 1 L/min and add regular nebulised salbutamol 2.5 mg every 20 minutes with careful cardiorespiratory monitoring
options.rationale: Salbutamol has no proven benefit in typical infant bronchiolitis and does not correct the ventilation deficit driving hypoxia and worsening work of breathing here.

options.text: Change to non-rebreather mask at 15 L/min and give nebulised adrenaline 5 mg with oral dexamethasone 0.6 mg/kg for prompt symptomatic relief
options.rationale: Non-rebreather masks are poorly tolerated in infants and give no positive pressure; adrenaline and steroid are croup pathway treatments, not bronchiolitis.

options.text: Continue nasal prong oxygen at 1 L/min and administer a 20 mL/kg normal saline bolus intravenously over 15 minutes to improve tissue perfusion
options.rationale: There is no shock: capillary refill is 2 seconds and lactate is normal. A fluid bolus risks worsening pulmonary oedema in bronchiolitis without indication.

options.text: Intubate and ventilate at pressure control 22/6 with FiO2 60 percent and admit to the local high dependency bed for ongoing ventilatory management
options.rationale: Intubation is premature before a trial of non-invasive escalation; PaCO2 48 with pH 7.34 is not immediate respiratory failure and HFNC or CPAP have not been tried.

explanation.summary: Infant bronchiolitis failing standard flow oxygen is escalated to heated humidified HFNC at 2 L/kg/min with FiO2 titrated to a target SpO2 of 92 to 96 percent. Salbutamol, adrenaline and steroids are not routine bronchiolitis therapies. Fluid boluses are reserved for shock, and intubation is a last resort after non-invasive support fails.
key_points: HFNC 2 L/kg/min is the first AU escalation for bronchiolitis with hypoxia
Bronchodilators, adrenaline and steroids do not treat classic bronchiolitis
Fluid boluses only if shocked; NG feeds preferred otherwise
Escalate to CPAP or intubate only after HFNC failure
explanation.pearls: In an infant on HFNC, heart rate that has not fallen and respiratory rate still above 60 after 60 minutes predicts HFNC failure and prompts CPAP or intubation planning.

stem: A 3-year-old Aboriginal boy presents to your remote community clinic with 24 hours of right ear pain, fever to 38.5 C and irritability. He has had two prior otitis media episodes this year. On otoscopy the right tympanic membrane is bulging, red and opaque without perforation. He is systemically well, feeding, alert and drinking normally with no mastoid tenderness and no facial nerve involvement.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 118, RR 24, SpO2 99 percent, temp 38.5 C
data_table.Examination: Right TM bulging, red, opaque; no perforation, no discharge; contralateral TM normal; no mastoid swelling; hydration adequate

lead_in: What is the most appropriate antibiotic decision?

options.text: Symptomatic treatment with paracetamol only and review in 48 hours to reassess before starting any antibiotic therapy for the ear infection
options.rationale: Watchful waiting is inappropriate here because he is Aboriginal and remote, a group at very high risk of chronic suppurative otitis media, where immediate antibiotics are recommended.

options.text: Oral amoxicillin 30 mg/kg twice daily for 7 days plus regular paracetamol for symptom relief, with safety-net review in 48 hours if not improving
options.rationale: AU guidance recommends immediate high-dose amoxicillin for 7 days in Aboriginal children, children under 2 years, or those with bilateral or severe disease. High-dose amoxicillin covers penicillin-non-susceptible pneumococcus.

options.text: Oral amoxicillin 15 mg/kg three times daily for 5 days plus regular paracetamol for symptomatic relief throughout the treatment course
options.rationale: For Aboriginal, remote, or under-2 children immediate high-dose amoxicillin is first line, and the standard course length in this group is 7 days rather than 5.

options.text: Oral amoxicillin-clavulanate 22.5 mg/kg twice daily for 7 days as first line to cover beta-lactamase producing pathogens implicated in recurrent disease
options.rationale: Amoxicillin-clavulanate is reserved for treatment failure at 48 to 72 hours or documented recurrence; high-dose amoxicillin monotherapy is first line for uncomplicated disease.

options.text: Intramuscular ceftriaxone 50 mg/kg as a single dose plus oral paracetamol and clinical review in the community clinic the following day
options.rationale: IM ceftriaxone is reserved for children unable to tolerate oral therapy or those with treatment failure; it is not first line in a well child able to take oral medication.

explanation.summary: Australian guidance treats Aboriginal children, children under 2 years, and children with bilateral or severe acute otitis media with immediate high-dose amoxicillin for 7 days because of high risk of chronic suppurative otitis media and pneumococcal complications. Watchful waiting is only for well older children in low-risk populations. Amoxicillin-clavulanate is reserved for treatment failure at 48 to 72 hours.
key_points: Immediate amoxicillin for Aboriginal, under-2, or severe or bilateral disease
High-dose amoxicillin 30 mg/kg BD covers non-susceptible pneumococcus
Course length is 7 days in high-risk groups
Amoxicillin-clavulanate reserved for treatment failure
explanation.pearls: Always examine both TMs and note any perforation size and discharge; a perforation with discharge changes management to topical ciprofloxacin drops alongside oral amoxicillin.

sources.label: CARPA Standard Treatment Manual: Ear infections

stem: A 5-year-old girl presents to your general practice with 6 months of hard infrequent bowel motions, faecal soiling of her underwear four times a week, and abdominal pain. On abdominal examination there is a firm indentable mass in the left iliac fossa reaching to the umbilicus. There is no vomiting, growth is on the 50th centile, and there is no history of delayed passage of meconium.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 92, RR 18, temp 36.7 C, weight 18 kg
data_table.Examination: Alert well-hydrated child; abdomen soft with palpable faecal mass in left iliac fossa; perianal skin intact; no anal fissure seen on inspection

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first step in management?

options.text: Refer to paediatric surgery for a manual disimpaction under general anaesthesia within the next two weeks in her local paediatric surgical service
options.rationale: Manual disimpaction under GA is reserved for children who fail oral or rectal disimpaction after several days; oral therapy is first line and effective in most children.

options.text: Prescribe daily microlax rectal enemas for 3 days plus a fibre-rich diet and increased fluids while awaiting response before further review
options.rationale: Rectal enemas are second line after oral macrogol has failed or been refused; they are more distressing for the child and family and are not more effective than oral macrogol.

options.text: Escalating oral macrogol regimen starting at 4 sachets on day 1 and increasing by 2 sachets daily for up to 7 days until liquid stool is passed
options.rationale: AU paediatric guidance recommends escalating oral macrogol as first-line disimpaction, titrated by weight and age to a ceiling around 12 sachets per day, over 3 to 7 days until liquid stool is passed.

options.text: Prescribe daily lactulose 10 mL twice daily and review her again in 4 weeks to reassess symptoms, stool pattern and any need for further therapy
options.rationale: Lactulose alone is inadequate for disimpaction; a maintenance dose osmotic laxative will not clear established faecal loading, and 4 weeks allows further soiling.

options.text: Arrange abdominal x-ray and rectal biopsy to exclude Hirschsprung disease and other structural causes before starting any pharmacological therapy for constipation
options.rationale: Hirschsprung disease presents with delayed meconium and failure to thrive from infancy, absent here. Imaging and biopsy are not needed to start therapy for typical functional constipation.

explanation.summary: Functional constipation with faecal loading is treated with escalating oral macrogol as first line disimpaction, titrated over 3 to 7 days until liquid stool is passed. Rectal enemas are second line and manual disimpaction under GA is rare. Investigations for organic causes are pursued only when red flags such as delayed meconium, failure to thrive, or abnormal perianal exam are present.
key_points: Escalating oral macrogol is first line disimpaction
Rectal enemas are second line, not first line
Maintenance osmotic laxatives will not clear an established impaction
Hirschsprung suspected only with delayed meconium and failure to thrive
explanation.pearls: Continue maintenance macrogol for at least 3 months after regular painless stools resume; earlier withdrawal is the commonest reason for relapse of soiling.

stem: A 6-year-old boy weighing 22 kg presents to your emergency department 20 minutes after eating a peanut biscuit. He has facial swelling, an urticarial rash on his chest, hoarse voice and stridor at rest. His mother has an EpiPen Jr (150 microgram) at home but did not use it. He has no cardiovascular collapse, IV access has just been secured, and he has no history of asthma.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 148, BP 92/60, RR 34, SpO2 94 percent room air, temp 36.9 C
data_table.Examination: Facial and lip swelling, hoarse voice, stridor at rest, widespread urticaria; chest with mild wheeze; capillary refill 2 seconds

lead_in: What is the immediate adrenaline dose and route you would give?

options.text: Adrenaline 150 microgram intramuscular into the mid-anterolateral thigh, repeated every 5 minutes if no response and rising respiratory distress
options.rationale: 150 microgram is the paediatric autoinjector for children 7.5 to 20 kg; this child is 22 kg so weight-based IM dose is 220 microgram, given as an autoinjector or 0.22 mL 1:1000.
source_refs: ASCIA Guidelines: Acute management of anaphylaxis

options.text: Adrenaline 300 microgram intravenous bolus given over 60 seconds, then commence a maintenance intravenous infusion at 0.1 microgram/kg/min for sustained cover
options.rationale: IV bolus adrenaline is not first line and carries significant risk of arrhythmia and hypertensive crisis; IM adrenaline is first line and IV infusion is reserved for refractory anaphylaxis.
source_refs: ASCIA Guidelines: Acute management of anaphylaxis

options.text: Adrenaline 500 microgram intramuscular into the deltoid muscle, repeated every 5 minutes if no adequate response to the initial dose is observed
options.rationale: 500 microgram is the adult IM dose; the deltoid is not the preferred site because absorption is slower than the mid-anterolateral thigh.
source_refs: ASCIA Guidelines: Acute management of anaphylaxis

options.text: Adrenaline 220 microgram intramuscular into the mid-anterolateral thigh (0.22 mL of 1:1000), repeated every 5 minutes as needed if no clinical response
options.rationale: Weight-based IM adrenaline for anaphylaxis is 10 microgram/kg to a maximum 500 microgram; for 22 kg this is 220 microgram (0.22 mL of 1:1000) IM into the mid-anterolateral thigh.
source_refs: ASCIA Guidelines: Acute management of anaphylaxis

options.text: Adrenaline 220 microgram nebulised via 6 L/min oxygen mask, plus IV hydrocortisone 100 mg for airway swelling and cardiovascular protection during transport
options.rationale: Nebulised adrenaline is not first line for anaphylaxis and does not treat cardiovascular or systemic manifestations; IM adrenaline is the standard first line therapy.
source_refs: ASCIA Guidelines: Acute management of anaphylaxis

explanation.summary: Anaphylaxis is treated with IM adrenaline 10 microgram/kg (maximum 500 microgram) into the mid-anterolateral thigh, repeated every 5 minutes as needed. For a 22 kg child this is 220 microgram given as 0.22 mL of 1:1000. IV bolus adrenaline is arrhythmogenic and reserved for refractory cases where an infusion is being initiated in a monitored setting.
key_points: IM adrenaline 10 microgram/kg to max 500 microgram is first line
Mid-anterolateral thigh gives faster absorption than deltoid
IV bolus adrenaline carries arrhythmia risk and is not first line
Repeat IM dose at 5 minutes if inadequate response
explanation.pearls: After two IM doses without adequate response, commence a peripheral adrenaline infusion at 0.1 to 1 microgram/kg/min while awaiting central access and senior support.

stem: A previously well 4-year-old girl presents to your paediatric emergency department with a 3 day history of new petechiae and bruising, appearing after a viral illness 2 weeks earlier. She has no active mucosal bleeding, no melaena and no headache. Examination shows scattered petechiae on trunk and limbs, some shin ecchymoses, and no hepatosplenomegaly or lymphadenopathy. She feels well and is playing normally in the cubicle.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 96, RR 22, BP 100/62, SpO2 99 percent, temp 37.1 C
data_table.Examination: Petechiae trunk and limbs, wet purpura absent, no oral bleeding, no hepatosplenomegaly, no lymphadenopathy
data_table.Investigations: Hb 122, WCC 7.1, platelets 9 x 10^9/L, film shows large platelets and no blasts; coagulation studies normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Admit for a 5 day course of oral prednisolone 2 mg/kg daily and repeat the platelet count on day 5 before deciding on inpatient discharge
options.rationale: Corticosteroids are considered for wet purpura, active bleeding, or a rising bleeding score; asymptomatic petechial disease in a well child does not warrant steroid exposure and admission.

options.text: Admit for a single dose of IV immunoglobulin 0.8 g/kg over 6 hours and repeat platelet count at 24 hours to assess treatment response and safety
options.rationale: IVIG is reserved for significant bleeding or a high bleeding risk score (wet purpura, mucosal bleeding, or planned procedure); it is not indicated in asymptomatic petechial disease.

options.text: Admit for a single dose of anti-D immunoglobulin 50 microgram/kg intravenously as first-line therapy to raise the platelet count promptly overnight
options.rationale: Anti-D is limited to Rh-positive non-splenectomised children with intact haemoglobin and carries a risk of severe haemolysis; it is not first line for asymptomatic ITP in Australia.

options.text: Perform urgent bone marrow aspirate and trephine to exclude acute leukaemia before starting any specific therapy for the thrombocytopenia observed today
options.rationale: Bone marrow examination is not required in classic ITP with a normal film, normal WCC and no atypical features; it is reserved for atypical presentations or before some centres start steroids.

options.text: Discharge home on active observation with strict return precautions and follow up review in the outpatient paediatric clinic one week from today
options.rationale: AU guidance supports observation for asymptomatic or minor bleeding phenotype ITP regardless of platelet count, with head injury and wet purpura advice, in preference to routine drug therapy.

explanation.summary: In children ITP is a clinical diagnosis and platelet count alone does not drive therapy; the Buchanan bleeding score guides decisions. A well child with only cutaneous petechiae and no wet purpura or active bleeding is managed with observation, safety advice and outpatient review regardless of platelet count. Steroids, IVIG and anti-D are reserved for higher-grade bleeding phenotypes and bone marrow only if atypical.
key_points: Manage by bleeding phenotype, not by platelet count alone
Observation is first line for cutaneous-only bleeding
IVIG and steroids reserved for wet purpura or active bleeding
Bone marrow only if atypical features present
explanation.pearls: The Buchanan bleeding score grades from 0 (none) to 5 (life-threatening); scores of 3 or more (mucosal bleeding or worse) prompt IVIG or steroid therapy, not the platelet count.

stem: A 12-year-old girl with new onset type 1 diabetes has completed 20 hours of DKA management on your paediatric high dependency unit. She weighs 44 kg and is on an IV insulin infusion at 0.05 units/kg/hour with maintenance fluids and dextrose. She is fully alert, tolerating oral fluids, hungry, and has passed urine three times. Venous gas pH 7.34, bicarbonate 18 mmol/L, beta-hydroxybutyrate 0.4 mmol/L, glucose 9.2 mmol/L.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 92, BP 118/70, RR 16, SpO2 99 percent, temp 36.8 C
data_table.Examination: Fully alert, well hydrated, no abdominal tenderness, no Kussmaul breathing, no focal neurology
data_table.Investigations: Venous pH 7.34, bicarbonate 18 mmol/L, glucose 9.2 mmol/L, ketones 0.4 mmol/L, sodium 138, potassium 4.1

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in insulin management?

options.text: Give subcutaneous long-acting insulin glargine 0.3 units/kg now, continue the IV insulin infusion for 2 hours, then stop the infusion at breakfast time
options.rationale: AU DKA guidance transitions once pH is above 7.3, bicarbonate above 15 and ketones under 1: give SC basal insulin, continue the IV infusion for at least 60 minutes for basal onset, then stop at a meal.

options.text: Cease the IV insulin infusion now and commence oral carbohydrate with correction doses of rapid-acting insulin only given when the meals are actually eaten
options.rationale: Ceasing IV insulin before subcutaneous insulin has taken effect leaves an unopposed gap that causes rebound ketosis; overlap between IV and SC insulin is required.

options.text: Increase the IV insulin infusion to 0.1 units/kg/hour and continue at this higher rate for another 6 hours before attempting subcutaneous transition to insulin
options.rationale: Acidosis and ketosis have already resolved; increasing the infusion rate now causes hypoglycaemia and delays her discharge planning without clinical benefit.

options.text: Give a single subcutaneous dose of rapid-acting insulin lispro 0.15 units/kg, cease IV infusion 15 minutes later and place her nil by mouth for observation
options.rationale: Rapid-acting insulin alone does not provide basal cover and nil by mouth removes the carbohydrate that mealtime bolus insulin is intended to cover; basal insulin is required.

options.text: Continue the IV insulin infusion overnight and reassess for subcutaneous transition when the endocrine consultant reviews her in the morning ward round
options.rationale: Prolonging the infusion after resolution wastes HDU resources, delays education and diet, and offers no clinical benefit once acidosis and ketosis have cleared.

explanation.summary: DKA resolves when pH exceeds 7.3, bicarbonate 15 mmol/L, and beta-hydroxybutyrate is under 1 mmol/L, with the child alert and tolerating oral intake. Transition is achieved by giving subcutaneous basal insulin (glargine or detemir), overlapping the IV insulin infusion for 60 to 120 minutes so basal insulin takes effect. The infusion is then stopped at a meal when a rapid-acting bolus is also given. Ceasing IV insulin without this overlap produces rebound ketosis, and rapid-acting insulin alone cannot substitute for basal cover.
key_points: Resolution: pH > 7.3, HCO3 > 15, ketones < 1 mmol/L, oral tolerating
Give basal SC insulin then overlap IV for 60 to 120 minutes
Never cease IV insulin without overlap or ketosis returns
Time the switch to a meal so rapid-acting cover can begin
explanation.pearls: For a newly diagnosed child, an initial total daily dose of 0.7 to 1.0 units/kg split as 40 to 50 percent basal glargine and the remainder as prandial rapid-acting is a reasonable starting regimen.

subtopic_detail: Nephrotic syndrome first relapse steroid regimen
stem: A 6-year-old boy with steroid-sensitive nephrotic syndrome, in remission for 4 months after his initial 12 week prednisolone course, presents to your general paediatric clinic with 3 days of periorbital swelling and morning-tested urinary protein 3 plus on dipstick at home. He is well with normal blood pressure and passing urine normally. Weight is 24 kg. There is no history of thromboembolism or infection.

data_table.Examination: Periorbital and mild pretibial oedema, no ascites, no scrotal oedema, chest clear
data_table.Investigations: Urine dipstick protein 3+; serum albumin 22 g/L; creatinine 40 micromol/L (baseline 40)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate steroid regimen for this first relapse?

options.text: Oral prednisolone 60 mg/m2 daily for 6 weeks, then 40 mg/m2 alternate days for 6 weeks and taper over a further 8 weeks over subsequent visits
options.rationale: This is the initial presentation regimen (extended 12 week course), not the shorter first-relapse regimen used once a child has already had induction therapy.
source_refs: KDIGO 2021 GN guideline: Nephrotic syndrome in children

options.text: Oral prednisolone 60 mg/m2 daily until urine is protein-free for 3 consecutive days, then 40 mg/m2 on alternate days for 4 weeks and then stop
options.rationale: This is the standard AU first-relapse regimen: daily prednisolone at 60 mg/m2 until 3 consecutive days of protein-free urine, then alternate day 40 mg/m2 for 4 weeks and cease.
source_refs: KDIGO 2021 GN guideline: Nephrotic syndrome in children

options.text: Oral cyclophosphamide 2 mg/kg daily for 12 weeks with pneumocystis prophylaxis, as prednisolone should be avoided in this first-relapse presentation for now
options.rationale: Cyclophosphamide is reserved for frequent relapsers or steroid-dependent disease, not for a single first relapse in a previously well-controlled child.
source_refs: KDIGO 2021 GN guideline: Nephrotic syndrome in children

options.text: Intravenous methylprednisolone 500 mg/m2 daily for 3 days, then oral prednisolone 60 mg/m2 daily for 4 weeks and review the case for renal biopsy referral
options.rationale: IV methylprednisolone pulses and biopsy are considered for steroid-resistant nephrotic syndrome, not a steroid-sensitive first relapse in a child previously responsive to oral steroids.
source_refs: KDIGO 2021 GN guideline: Nephrotic syndrome in children

options.text: Oral tacrolimus 0.1 mg/kg twice daily aiming for a trough level of 4 to 8 microgram/L and cease prednisolone entirely to avoid growth impact for now
options.rationale: Calcineurin inhibitors are steroid-sparing agents reserved for frequent-relapsing or steroid-dependent disease, not a first relapse in a previously stable child on prednisolone.
source_refs: KDIGO 2021 GN guideline: Nephrotic syndrome in children

explanation.summary: First relapse of steroid-sensitive nephrotic syndrome is treated with oral prednisolone 60 mg/m2 daily until three consecutive days of urine protein-free, then 40 mg/m2 on alternate days for 4 weeks and stop. Extended 12 week courses are reserved for the initial presentation. Steroid-sparing agents such as cyclophosphamide or calcineurin inhibitors are added only for frequent relapses or steroid dependence.
key_points: First relapse: 60 mg/m2 daily until 3 days protein-free, then 40 mg/m2 alt-day 4 weeks
Initial presentation regimen is longer and should not be re-used
Cyclophosphamide, tacrolimus for frequent relapse or steroid dependence
Biopsy only if steroid-resistant or atypical
explanation.pearls: Steroid dependence is defined as two consecutive relapses during taper or within 14 days of ceasing; frequent-relapsing is 2 relapses in 6 months or 4 in 12 months, either of which prompts steroid-sparing discussion.

sources.label: KDIGO 2021 GN guideline: Nephrotic syndrome in children

stem: A 3-day-old term male infant is brought to your regional emergency department after collapsing at home during a feed. He is grey, mottled and floppy. Femoral pulses are absent and brachial pulses weak. Urgent echocardiogram by the paediatric cardiology fellow shows critical coarctation with a restrictive ductus arteriosus. You commence PGE1 at 0.05 microgram/kg/min. Over 30 minutes SpO2 rises to 88 percent but he becomes progressively apnoeic, hypotonic and temperature drops to 35.4 C. Weight 3.2 kg.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 172, BP 54/28 (right arm), SpO2 pre-ductal 82 to 88 percent, post-ductal 76 percent, temp 35.4 C, RR now 6
data_table.Examination: Grey infant, apnoeic episodes 20 seconds, capillary refill 4 seconds, femoral pulses now palpable, brachial pulses stronger
data_table.Investigations: Venous pH 7.18, lactate 6.8 mmol/L, glucose 3.4 mmol/L, potassium 4.9 mmol/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in his airway and infusion management?

options.text: Reduce the PGE1 infusion to 0.01 microgram/kg/min and continue high flow nasal cannula oxygen at 2 L/kg/min for further ventilatory support and stabilisation
options.rationale: Apnoea from PGE1 requires airway control not dose reduction alone; the duct is only just opening and dose reduction without airway support risks re-closure and unsupported apnoea.
source_refs: NETS retrieval guideline: Neonatal cardiac emergencies

options.text: Give caffeine citrate 20 mg/kg IV as loading dose, continue nasal prong oxygen and continue PGE1 at 0.05 microgram/kg/min for the retrieval transfer
options.rationale: Caffeine has slow onset and does not reliably prevent PGE1-induced apnoea; established apnoea with dropping temperature and rising lactate requires definitive airway control before transport.
source_refs: NETS retrieval guideline: Neonatal cardiac emergencies

options.text: Intubate and ventilate now, continue PGE1 at 0.05 microgram/kg/min, then titrate the infusion down to the lowest effective dose of 0.01 to 0.02 microgram/kg/min
options.rationale: PGE1-induced apnoea is expected: once ductal patency and pre and post-ductal oxygenation are confirmed the infusion can be titrated down to the lowest effective dose while the airway is safely controlled by intubation.
source_refs: NETS retrieval guideline: Neonatal cardiac emergencies

options.text: Cease PGE1 infusion, give a 20 mL/kg normal saline fluid bolus and administer IV adrenaline 10 microgram/kg for the cardiovascular shock and hypoperfusion
options.rationale: Ceasing PGE1 will close the duct and cause immediate collapse in a ductal-dependent lesion; the priority here is airway control and continuing PGE1, not adrenaline.
source_refs: NETS retrieval guideline: Neonatal cardiac emergencies

options.text: Increase PGE1 to 0.1 microgram/kg/min for maximal ductal patency, apply CPAP 5 cm H2O and rewarm the infant using a radiant warmer during preparation for transfer
options.rationale: Higher dose PGE1 increases apnoea, fever and hypotension without additional ductal benefit once patency is achieved; the maintenance dose window is 0.01 to 0.02 microgram/kg/min.
source_refs: NETS retrieval guideline: Neonatal cardiac emergencies

explanation.summary: PGE1 opens and maintains a patent ductus arteriosus in ductal-dependent lesions such as critical coarctation. Higher initial doses of 0.05 to 0.1 microgram/kg/min are used to reopen a closed duct; once patency is confirmed the infusion is titrated to the lowest effective dose of 0.01 to 0.02 microgram/kg/min to minimise apnoea, hypotension and vasodilatation. Intubation before transfer is standard practice.
key_points: Reopen closed duct with 0.05 to 0.1 microgram/kg/min PGE1
Once open, titrate to 0.01 to 0.02 microgram/kg/min lowest effective dose
Apnoea, hypotension, fever and flushing are dose-related side effects
Intubate before retrieval; do not rely on caffeine or CPAP alone
explanation.pearls: In critical coarctation, aim for pre-ductal SpO2 around 75 to 85 percent to balance Qp and Qs; higher pre-ductal SpO2 risks systemic hypoperfusion from pulmonary steal.

sources.label: NETS retrieval guideline: Neonatal cardiac emergencies
