subtopic_detail: Intrapartum GBS prophylaxis in preterm labour
stem: A 27-year-old G2P1 woman at 32+2 weeks presents to your labour ward with regular painful contractions every 4 minutes. Vaginal examination shows the cervix 4 cm dilated and fully effaced. Membranes are intact. Her last GBS swab was negative at 26 weeks in her previous pregnancy; no GBS swab has been performed in this pregnancy. She has no penicillin allergy and no other risk factors for infection. Fetal heart rate is reassuring.

data_table.Examination: Cervix 4 cm dilated, fully effaced, membranes intact; regular contractions every 4 minutes; fundus at 33 cm; presenting part cephalic at station -2

lead_in: What is the most appropriate antibiotic decision for GBS prophylaxis?

options.text: No intrapartum antibiotics as her previous pregnancy swab was negative and there are no additional risk factors present in this pregnancy so far
options.rationale: A GBS swab from a previous pregnancy does not carry over; preterm labour without a current negative GBS status is treated as GBS positive with intrapartum penicillin.
source_refs: RANZCOG: Prevention of early-onset neonatal GBS disease

options.text: Take a low vaginal and rectal swab now for GBS PCR and defer intravenous antibiotics until the result is available in approximately 4 hours from now
options.rationale: Delivery is imminent at 4 cm and four-minutely contractions; delaying antibiotics for a PCR result risks inadequate cover and PCR has variable turnaround times.
source_refs: RANZCOG: Prevention of early-onset neonatal GBS disease

options.text: Give IV amoxicillin 2 g loading dose then 1 g every four hours plus IV gentamicin 5 mg/kg once daily for broad-spectrum cover during her labour
options.rationale: Broad-spectrum cover including gentamicin is used for clinical chorioamnionitis, not intrapartum GBS prophylaxis in a woman without infection features.
source_refs: RANZCOG: Prevention of early-onset neonatal GBS disease

options.text: IV benzylpenicillin 3 g loading dose then 1.8 g every 4 hours until delivery, treating preterm labour without a current negative GBS status as GBS positive
options.rationale: AU RANZCOG guidance treats preterm labour under 37 weeks without a current negative GBS status as GBS positive; benzylpenicillin 3 g load then 1.8 g four-hourly is the regimen.
source_refs: RANZCOG: Prevention of early-onset neonatal GBS disease

options.text: Give IV clindamycin 900 mg every eight hours until delivery, as clindamycin covers GBS reliably regardless of the culture status in this preterm patient
options.rationale: Clindamycin is used only when penicillin is contraindicated and only after confirming isolate susceptibility; up to 20 percent of GBS isolates in AU are resistant.
source_refs: RANZCOG: Prevention of early-onset neonatal GBS disease

explanation.summary: Preterm labour before 37 weeks without a current negative GBS status is managed as GBS positive with intrapartum penicillin. The standard regimen is benzylpenicillin 3 g IV load then 1.8 g four-hourly until delivery. A prior pregnancy swab does not carry across. In true penicillin allergy cefazolin is used for low-risk anaphylaxis and clindamycin only if the isolate is confirmed susceptible.
key_points: Preterm labour without current negative GBS swab is treated as GBS positive
Prior pregnancy GBS swab does not carry over
Regimen: benzylpenicillin 3 g load then 1.8 g Q4H until delivery
Clindamycin only if penicillin allergy AND susceptible isolate
explanation.pearls: In severe penicillin allergy (anaphylaxis), request GBS susceptibility on any available swab before defaulting to clindamycin; up to 20 percent of AU GBS isolates are clindamycin resistant and vancomycin becomes the alternative.

sources.label: RANZCOG: Prevention of early-onset neonatal GBS disease

subtopic_detail: Anti-D immunoglobulin dosing for sensitising event
stem: A 29-year-old G2P1 RhD-negative woman at 15 weeks gestation presents to your emergency department 4 hours after a moderate abdominal blow from a motor vehicle accident. She has mild lower abdominal tenderness but no vaginal bleeding. Ultrasound shows a live fetus with normal fetal heart rate and no retroplacental clot. She is otherwise well. Her partner is RhD-positive and she is confirmed RhD-negative on her routine antenatal group and screen.

data_table.Examination: Mild lower abdominal tenderness, no vaginal bleeding, fundus not palpable abdominally at this gestation
data_table.Investigations: Group and hold: O-negative; antibody screen negative; ultrasound live fetus, no retroplacental clot

lead_in: What is the most appropriate anti-D dose and Kleihauer approach?

options.text: No anti-D immunoglobulin is required as there is no visible vaginal bleeding and ultrasound shows no retroplacental clot on this presentation today
options.rationale: Any potentially sensitising event including abdominal trauma requires anti-D regardless of visible bleeding; feto-maternal haemorrhage may occur without external signs.

options.text: Administer 250 IU (50 microgram) intramuscular anti-D immunoglobulin now with no Kleihauer required at this gestation, then routine follow-up in clinic
options.rationale: 250 IU is the standard dose for sensitising events before 12 weeks; at 15 weeks the standard sensitising event dose is 625 IU, and Kleihauer is not required before 20 weeks.

options.text: Administer 625 IU (125 microgram) IM anti-D immunoglobulin now and request Kleihauer to determine any additional dose required for the sensitising event today
options.rationale: Kleihauer is required at or after 20 weeks only; before 20 weeks a single standard dose reliably covers the expected feto-maternal haemorrhage volume.

options.text: Administer 1500 IU IM anti-D immunoglobulin now and repeat 625 IU every 6 weeks until delivery in view of the trauma and the perceived ongoing risk
options.rationale: 1500 IU is the routine antenatal prophylactic dose given at 28 and 34 weeks; the sensitising event dose at this gestation is 625 IU, not 1500.

options.text: Administer 625 IU (125 microgram) intramuscular anti-D immunoglobulin now, and Kleihauer testing is not required at gestations before 20 weeks
options.rationale: AU NBA advice is 625 IU IM anti-D for sensitising events from 12 weeks up to and including delivery; Kleihauer is not needed before 20 weeks as the standard dose covers likely feto-maternal haemorrhage.

explanation.summary: In an RhD-negative pregnant woman, any potentially sensitising event including abdominal trauma requires anti-D immunoglobulin. Before 12 weeks the dose is 250 IU IM; from 12 weeks the dose is 625 IU IM. Kleihauer testing is not required before 20 weeks because a single 625 IU dose neutralises any likely feto-maternal haemorrhage volume; at or after 20 weeks Kleihauer guides additional doses.
key_points: Any sensitising event triggers anti-D regardless of visible bleeding
Under 12 weeks 250 IU; from 12 weeks 625 IU IM
Kleihauer required only at 20 weeks or later
Routine antenatal prophylaxis is 1500 IU at 28 and 34 weeks
explanation.pearls: Sensitising events include amniocentesis, external cephalic version, antepartum haemorrhage and abdominal trauma; give anti-D within 72 hours of the event but a dose given within 10 days still offers partial protection.

stem: A 62-year-old woman who reached menopause at age 51 presents to your gynaecology clinic with one episode of light postmenopausal bleeding 2 weeks ago. She is not on hormone replacement therapy. Body mass index is 34 kg/m2 and she has type 2 diabetes. She has no vaginal atrophy on examination and no cervical lesion is visible. Her transvaginal ultrasound today shows an endometrial thickness of 6 mm with a smooth outline and no focal lesion.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 76, BP 138/84, RR 16, temp 36.7 C, BMI 34 kg/m2
data_table.Examination: External genitalia normal, no vaginal atrophy, cervix healthy on speculum, no lesion; bimanual normal size uterus, no adnexal masses
data_table.Investigations: TVUS endometrial thickness 6 mm, smooth outline, no focal lesion, ovaries normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in evaluation?

options.text: Arrange outpatient hysteroscopy with directed endometrial biopsy to obtain histological diagnosis of the thickened endometrium seen at transvaginal ultrasound today
options.rationale: Endometrial thickness greater than 4 mm in a postmenopausal woman with bleeding requires endometrial sampling. Outpatient hysteroscopy with biopsy is the preferred AU approach when available, especially in obesity and diabetes.

options.text: Reassure and discharge with safety-net advice, since an endometrial thickness under 10 mm makes malignancy very unlikely in this postmenopausal patient population
options.rationale: The AU RANZCOG threshold to reassure without tissue is 4 mm or less; at 6 mm with risk factors of obesity and diabetes, tissue diagnosis is required for safety.

options.text: Repeat transvaginal ultrasound in 6 weeks to assess for persistent thickening of the endometrium before considering endometrial biopsy or referral for hysteroscopy
options.rationale: A delay of 6 weeks in a symptomatic postmenopausal woman with an above threshold endometrium is inappropriate; tissue diagnosis is needed now to exclude malignancy.

options.text: Trial 3 months of vaginal oestrogen cream and review symptoms and endometrial thickness at the end of the treatment period before further investigation
options.rationale: Vaginal oestrogen would not be given to a woman with unexplained postmenopausal bleeding and could worsen an occult endometrial cancer if present under the endometrium.

options.text: Refer for MRI pelvis to further characterise the endometrium and adnexa before deciding whether an endometrial biopsy is required for tissue diagnosis at all
options.rationale: MRI is not first line; it is used for staging once endometrial malignancy has been histologically confirmed, not for the initial diagnostic decision in postmenopausal bleeding.

explanation.summary: Postmenopausal bleeding with a transvaginal ultrasound endometrial thickness greater than 4 mm requires endometrial sampling. Outpatient hysteroscopy with directed biopsy is preferred where available, particularly in women with high pretest probability such as obesity, diabetes, or Lynch syndrome. Blind pipelle sampling is acceptable when hysteroscopy is not immediately available.
key_points: PMB with endometrial thickness > 4 mm needs tissue diagnosis
Outpatient hysteroscopy plus biopsy preferred where available
Obesity, diabetes, unopposed oestrogen and tamoxifen raise pretest probability
Do not use vaginal oestrogen before diagnosis is made
explanation.pearls: In women with Lynch syndrome, endometrial cancer risk is high and screening should include annual endometrial biopsy and TVUS from age 35, not the 4 mm threshold applied to sporadic PMB.

subtopic_detail: Contraception choice in migraine with aura
stem: A 24-year-old woman presents to your general practice for contraception advice. She has migraine with aura, described as bilateral scintillating scotoma lasting 30 minutes preceding a headache, occurring about once monthly. She smokes 5 cigarettes daily. She has regular menstrual cycles and no other cardiovascular risk factors. Her BMI is 22 kg/m2 and her blood pressure is 118/72. She wants long-acting reversible contraception.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 72, BP 118/72, RR 14, BMI 22 kg/m2
data_table.Examination: Well woman, no focal neurology, cardiovascular examination normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate contraceptive option?

options.text: Combined oral contraceptive pill containing ethinyloestradiol 20 microgram and levonorgestrel 100 microgram taken daily for continuous cycle control
options.rationale: Migraine with aura is a UKMEC category 4 contraindication to combined hormonal contraception at any dose due to ischaemic stroke risk associated with oestrogen exposure.

options.text: Levonorgestrel intrauterine device (52 mg) inserted for 5 years, providing highly effective progestogen-only long-acting reversible contraception without oestrogen exposure
options.rationale: Progestogen-only intrauterine contraception is UKMEC category 1 in migraine with aura; it is highly effective, long-acting, reversible and does not carry the oestrogen-related ischaemic stroke risk.

options.text: Combined transdermal patch delivering ethinyloestradiol 20 microgram and norelgestromin 150 microgram daily for continuous contraceptive cover in the community
options.rationale: Any oestrogen-containing method is UKMEC category 4 in migraine with aura, regardless of the route of oestrogen administration used or the specific progestogen combined with it.

options.text: Depot medroxyprogesterone acetate 150 mg intramuscular every 12 weeks, starting today and continuing as long-term contraceptive cover through further clinic reviews
options.rationale: DMPA is UKMEC category 2 in migraine with aura and is a reasonable option, but is not as long-acting or as low-risk for bone loss and weight gain as a LNG-IUD.

options.text: Vaginal ring delivering ethinyloestradiol 15 microgram and etonogestrel 120 microgram daily, replaced every 3 weeks with a hormone-free week to allow bleeding
options.rationale: The vaginal ring contains oestrogen and remains UKMEC category 4 in migraine with aura; the route does not change the ischaemic stroke risk assessment for combined hormonal methods.

explanation.summary: Migraine with aura is a UKMEC category 4 contraindication to any oestrogen-containing contraception because of ischaemic stroke risk; this includes combined oral pill, patch and vaginal ring at any dose. Progestogen-only methods are safe. The levonorgestrel intrauterine device is UKMEC category 1, highly effective and long-acting, and is the preferred option here. DMPA is acceptable but has other drawbacks compared with an IUD.
key_points: Migraine with aura: UKMEC 4 for any oestrogen-containing method
LNG-IUD is UKMEC 1 and preferred LARC in aura
Progestogen-only pill and DMPA are UKMEC 2
Route of oestrogen (oral, patch, ring) does not change the category
explanation.pearls: Aura features that trigger UKMEC 4 include any focal neurological symptom lasting under 60 minutes (visual, sensory, dysphasia); a nonspecific prodrome or postdrome without focal neurology is not aura.

subtopic_detail: Planned caesarean for placenta accreta spectrum
stem: A 36-year-old G4P3 woman with three previous caesarean sections has an anterior placenta praevia at 32 weeks. MRI at 30 weeks shows features of placenta increta with focal loss of the retroplacental clear zone, bulging of placenta into bladder wall, and abnormal vascularity. She is stable with no bleeding. Delivery is being planned at your tertiary maternal-fetal medicine centre. She is fully counselled and has consented to caesarean hysterectomy if required.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 82, BP 122/76, RR 14, temp 36.8 C, BMI 32
data_table.Examination: Abdomen soft, fundus 32 cm, cephalic, no tenderness
data_table.Investigations: MRI 30 weeks: features of placenta increta; MSU negative; Hb 118, platelets 258; group and hold complete

lead_in: What is the most appropriate delivery planning strategy?

options.text: Planned classical caesarean under general anaesthesia at 39 weeks with immediate hysterectomy avoiding attempts at placental removal, with a 4 unit red cell cross-match
options.rationale: For placenta accreta spectrum, planned delivery is 34+0 to 35+6 weeks after antenatal steroids, not 39 weeks; delay to 39 weeks risks unscheduled bleeding and emergency surgery.

options.text: Continue expectant management with weekly ultrasound and plan for spontaneous labour with continuous fetal monitoring at term with a low threshold for emergency caesarean
options.rationale: Vaginal delivery is contraindicated with placenta praevia and accreta due to unmanageable haemorrhage risk; expectant management to term is unsafe in placenta accreta spectrum.

options.text: Planned caesarean hysterectomy at 34+0 to 35+6 weeks after antenatal corticosteroids, leaving placenta in situ, with MDT and IR standby and 4 to 6 unit cross-match
options.rationale: AU MFM guidance advises delivery between 34+0 and 35+6 weeks after antenatal steroids, with an MDT including anaesthesia, urology, IR and blood bank; the placenta is left in situ during hysterectomy.

options.text: Planned lower segment caesarean at 37 weeks with attempted manual removal of the placenta and bimanual compression plus uterotonic infusion if uterine bleeding occurs
options.rationale: Attempted manual removal in placenta accreta causes catastrophic haemorrhage; the placenta must be left in situ during hysterectomy or conservative management is chosen.

options.text: Planned classical caesarean at 34 weeks with insertion of a Rusch balloon before uterine closure to allow later delivery of the placenta 6 weeks postpartum
options.rationale: Delayed hysterectomy at 6 weeks is a conservative alternative in selected fertility-preserving cases; a Rusch balloon does not have a role and planned caesarean hysterectomy is standard.

explanation.summary: Placenta accreta spectrum is delivered by planned caesarean between 34+0 and 35+6 weeks after a course of antenatal corticosteroids, in a tertiary centre with an MDT including obstetric anaesthesia, urology, interventional radiology and blood bank. Cross-match at least 4 to 6 units of red cells. The placenta is left in situ during hysterectomy; attempted removal causes catastrophic haemorrhage.
key_points: Planned delivery 34+0 to 35+6 weeks after antenatal steroids
Do not attempt to remove the placenta at CS
MDT: MFM, anaesthesia, urology, IR, blood bank
Cross-match 4 to 6 units red cells minimum
explanation.pearls: For women declining hysterectomy who wish to preserve fertility, a Triple-P procedure or leaving the placenta in situ with methotrexate is an option, but with substantial infection and delayed bleeding risk.

stem: A 32-year-old G1P0 woman at 32 weeks has a transvaginal ultrasound today for a low-lying placenta, which has now migrated. However, colour Doppler shows fetal vessels running through membranes over the internal cervical os, confirming vasa praevia. She has had no bleeding, is asymptomatic and cervical length is 34 mm. Fetal movements are normal and fetal growth is at the 50th centile.

data_table.Examination: Fundus 32 cm, cephalic presentation, no vaginal bleeding
data_table.Investigations: TVUS: vasa praevia confirmed with fetal vessels overlying internal os, cervical length 34 mm, EFW 50th centile

lead_in: What is the most appropriate antenatal management plan?

options.text: Continue routine antenatal care with delivery by elective caesarean at 39 weeks and expectant management until then, with fetal movement education for the mother
options.rationale: 39 weeks is too late; the risk of membrane rupture and fetal exsanguination rises after 34 weeks. Inpatient admission and steroids are usually recommended from around 32 weeks.

options.text: Inpatient admission from 32 weeks with betamethasone 11.4 mg IM twice 24 hours apart, then elective caesarean at 39 weeks unless she develops any bleeding beforehand
options.rationale: Waiting to 39 weeks after admission and steroids exposes the pregnancy to spontaneous rupture and fetal exsanguination; planned delivery is at 34+0 to 35+6 weeks after steroids.

options.text: Outpatient management with weekly cardiotocography and TVUS until 37 weeks, at which point an elective caesarean is performed under regional anaesthesia after discussion
options.rationale: Outpatient management to 37 weeks exposes the pregnancy to risk of membrane rupture during transit; inpatient admission and earlier planned delivery are preferred.

options.text: Inpatient admission from 32 weeks with betamethasone 11.4 mg IM in two doses 24 hours apart, then elective caesarean at 34+0 to 35+6 weeks
options.rationale: AU RANZCOG supports inpatient admission around 32 weeks, antenatal steroids completing before 34 weeks, and elective caesarean at 34+0 to 35+6 weeks before spontaneous rupture and haemorrhage can occur.

options.text: Immediate emergency caesarean at 32 weeks under general anaesthesia given the risk of catastrophic haemorrhage from any spontaneous membrane rupture that might occur
options.rationale: Immediate delivery at 32 weeks exposes the neonate to unnecessary preterm complications; the risk-benefit balance favours planned delivery at 34 to 36 weeks after steroids.

explanation.summary: Confirmed vasa praevia requires planned inpatient admission around 32 weeks with a course of antenatal corticosteroids completed before 34 weeks. Elective caesarean is performed at 34+0 to 35+6 weeks before spontaneous rupture of membranes can cause fetal exsanguination. Outpatient management to term risks membrane rupture in transit and is not standard AU practice. Immediate delivery at 32 weeks unnecessarily commits the neonate to preterm complications when planned delivery a few weeks later is safer.
key_points: Confirmed vasa praevia: admit around 32 weeks, steroids, deliver 34 to 36 weeks
Vaginal delivery contraindicated
Outpatient management to term is not standard
Emergency caesarean if any ROM or bleeding regardless of gestation
explanation.pearls: A 50 mL fetal bleed can exsanguinate a term fetus; do not wait for an abnormal CTG. If membranes rupture with bleeding, category 1 caesarean is warranted for suspected vasa praevia bleeding.

subtopic_detail: Ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome grade and management
stem: A 34-year-old woman, day 8 after oocyte retrieval, presents to your emergency department with abdominal distension, oliguria and calf pain. She underwent IVF with 25 oocytes retrieved. She is dyspnoeic on exertion. Weight is up 4 kg since collection. On examination she has tense ascites and reduced air entry at the right lung base with dullness to percussion. Serum sodium 129, potassium 5.4, creatinine 130, haematocrit 0.51.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 118, BP 100/62, RR 24, SpO2 93 percent, temp 37.2 C
data_table.Examination: Tense ascites, right pleural effusion clinically, calf oedema and tenderness left leg, no chest pain
data_table.Investigations: Na 129, K 5.4, creatinine 130, haematocrit 0.51, WCC 16, platelets 420; urine output 20 mL/hour over 6 hours

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Discharge home on 3 litres oral fluids daily, oral cabergoline 0.5 mg twice weekly for 8 weeks, and a follow-up specialist appointment in the fertility clinic tomorrow
options.rationale: Cabergoline is a preventative pre-trigger measure; this severe hospital-requiring presentation cannot be safely managed as an outpatient with oral therapy and follow-up.

options.text: IV furosemide 40 mg for the fluid overload plus 3 litres of normal saline over 6 hours to improve renal perfusion and correct the low urine output during observation
options.rationale: Furosemide worsens intravascular depletion and haemoconcentration in OHSS; loop diuretics are contraindicated in the third-space phase of the illness where extravascular fluid predominates.

options.text: Commence therapeutic anticoagulation with enoxaparin 1 mg/kg twice daily for suspected pulmonary embolism and proceed to CT pulmonary angiogram for further evaluation
options.rationale: Prophylactic-dose enoxaparin is standard for severe OHSS; therapeutic dose is reserved for confirmed VTE and CT-PA is only warranted if suspicion is high, not from ascites-related dyspnoea alone.

options.text: Prescribe oral spironolactone 100 mg daily, restrict oral fluid intake to 800 mL per day and follow up as an outpatient in 3 days for repeat electrolyte assessment and review
options.rationale: Fluid restriction and diuretics worsen haemoconcentration and thrombotic risk in severe OHSS; outpatient care is inappropriate with haematocrit above 0.45 plus oliguria and tense ascites.

options.text: Admit for cautious IV crystalloid, prophylactic-dose enoxaparin, human albumin infusion for oncotic support, and ultrasound-guided paracentesis if respiratory compromise persists
options.rationale: Severe OHSS with tense ascites, oliguria, haemoconcentration and effusion requires admission with careful crystalloid or colloid, VTE prophylaxis and paracentesis for symptomatic relief.

explanation.summary: Severe OHSS with tense ascites, oliguria, haemoconcentration (haematocrit above 0.45) and pleural effusion requires hospital admission. Manage with cautious IV crystalloid or colloid to restore intravascular volume, human albumin as oncotic support, prophylactic-dose enoxaparin (severe OHSS is a strong VTE risk), and ultrasound-guided paracentesis for symptomatic ascites or effusion. Diuretics and fluid restriction are contraindicated as they worsen haemoconcentration and thrombosis.
key_points: Severe OHSS: admit, cautious IV fluids, VTE prophylaxis
Paracentesis for symptomatic tense ascites or effusion
Diuretics contraindicated in third-space phase
Cabergoline is a preventive measure, not a treatment at this stage
explanation.pearls: Cabergoline 0.5 mg daily started on the day of hCG trigger for 8 days reduces the incidence of moderate-to-severe OHSS by modulating VEGF-mediated vascular permeability.

stem: A 30-year-old woman presents to your emergency department 8 days postpartum after a delivery complicated by placental abruption with 2.8 L blood loss and 6 units red cell transfusion. Today she is drowsy, hypotensive, hypoglycaemic and hyponatraemic. She has failed to lactate. Random cortisol 42 nmol/L, TSH 0.6 mIU/L, free T4 8 pmol/L, sodium 122 mmol/L, glucose 2.6 mmol/L. She is drowsy but rousable.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 108, BP 84/50, RR 20, SpO2 97 percent, temp 35.9 C
data_table.Examination: Drowsy but rousable, GCS 13, cool peripheries, capillary refill 3 seconds; breasts not lactating; no goitre, no adrenal skin pigmentation
data_table.Investigations: Cortisol 42 nmol/L, TSH 0.6 mIU/L, free T4 8 pmol/L, Na 122, K 4.1, glucose 2.6, Hb 92

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate hormone replacement order?

options.text: IV hydrocortisone 100 mg every 6 hours first, IV 10 percent dextrose for hypoglycaemia, cautious 3 percent saline for symptomatic hyponatraemia, then thyroxine after 24 hours
options.rationale: In panhypopituitarism, glucocorticoid replacement must precede thyroxine to avoid precipitating adrenal crisis, along with dextrose for hypoglycaemia and cautious hypertonic saline for symptomatic hyponatraemia.
source_refs: Endocrine Society: Diagnosis and treatment of hypopituitarism

options.text: Give IV levothyroxine 200 microgram now, followed by oral levothyroxine 100 microgram daily, then IV hydrocortisone 100 mg six-hourly to complete the replacement
options.rationale: Thyroxine before glucocorticoid replacement in panhypopituitarism can precipitate adrenal crisis by increasing metabolic demand on unreplaced cortisol; steroids must be given first.
source_refs: Endocrine Society: Diagnosis and treatment of hypopituitarism

options.text: IV hydrocortisone 100 mg every 6 hours, avoid dextrose and hypertonic saline as these overcorrect the sodium too rapidly, and defer thyroxine replacement indefinitely to prevent rebound
options.rationale: Symptomatic hypoglycaemia needs dextrose and severe symptomatic hyponatraemia at 122 warrants cautious hypertonic saline; deferring thyroxine indefinitely once cortisol is replaced is inappropriate.
source_refs: Endocrine Society: Diagnosis and treatment of hypopituitarism

options.text: Give fludrocortisone 100 microgram orally daily as first-line steroid, then oral levothyroxine 100 microgram once the mineralocorticoid effect has been established over 24 hours
options.rationale: Fludrocortisone is not required in secondary adrenal insufficiency since aldosterone secretion is preserved via the RAAS; hydrocortisone is the correct first agent for the cortisol deficit.
source_refs: Endocrine Society: Diagnosis and treatment of hypopituitarism

options.text: Give IV dexamethasone 8 mg and then perform a diagnostic short synacthen test before instituting any further hormone replacement therapy or dextrose or saline supplementation today
options.rationale: Delaying life-saving replacement to complete a synacthen test in a haemodynamically unstable postpartum woman is inappropriate; treat first and confirm the diagnosis later.
source_refs: Endocrine Society: Diagnosis and treatment of hypopituitarism

explanation.summary: Sheehan syndrome from postpartum haemorrhage causes panhypopituitarism with hypocortisolism, hypothyroidism and central diabetes insipidus in some patients. The immediate priority is hydrocortisone 100 mg IV every 6 hours to prevent adrenal crisis, correction of hypoglycaemia with dextrose, and cautious hypertonic saline for symptomatic hyponatraemia. Thyroxine must be started after glucocorticoid replacement because unopposed thyroxine can precipitate adrenal crisis.
key_points: Hydrocortisone before thyroxine in panhypopituitarism
Dextrose for hypoglycaemia, cautious hypertonic saline for symptomatic hyponatraemia
Fludrocortisone not required in secondary adrenal insufficiency
Synacthen test and other confirmatory tests come after treatment
explanation.pearls: The classical Sheehan triad of failure to lactate, secondary amenorrhoea and postural symptoms may not appear until months after the causative haemorrhage; a low index of suspicion for hypopituitarism in postpartum fatigue and hyponatraemia is warranted.

sources.label: Endocrine Society: Diagnosis and treatment of hypopituitarism

stem: A 34-year-old male veteran presents to your general practice with 8 months of intrusive memories of combat, hypervigilance, sleep disturbance and avoidance of crowds after his return from deployment. He meets criteria for post-traumatic stress disorder and has completed 8 sessions of trauma-focused cognitive behavioural therapy with partial response. He is not currently suicidal. He has no history of psychosis, bipolar disorder or substance dependence. He has agreed to add pharmacotherapy.

data_table.Examination: Alert, cooperative, mood low, no thought disorder, no suicidal ideation, no substance intoxication

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first-line pharmacotherapy?

options.text: Oral quetiapine 25 mg at night, titrated up to 300 mg daily total for management of hyperarousal, sleep disturbance and residual anxiety symptoms during the day
options.rationale: Second-generation antipsychotics are not first line for PTSD; quetiapine is considered only as an augmentation agent and its metabolic risks argue against routine use in this setting.

options.text: Oral sertraline 50 mg daily, titrated up to 100 to 200 mg daily based on response and tolerability over 4 to 6 weeks with symptom and side effect monitoring
options.rationale: AU RANZCP guidance recommends an SSRI (sertraline or paroxetine) as first-line pharmacotherapy for PTSD in adults, starting at 50 mg daily and titrating to a therapeutic dose over 4 to 6 weeks.

options.text: Oral benzodiazepine diazepam 5 mg three times daily to manage hyperarousal and improve sleep in the short term while awaiting response to psychological therapies
options.rationale: Benzodiazepines are contraindicated as first line in PTSD; they worsen extinction of trauma memories and carry dependence risk in a chronic condition like this.

options.text: Oral prazosin 1 mg at night titrated up to 5 mg for nightmares as first-line pharmacotherapy addressing the full spectrum of post-traumatic symptoms he is experiencing
options.rationale: Prazosin has a specific role for trauma-related nightmares but does not address the full PTSD symptom cluster; SSRIs remain first line by RCT evidence.

options.text: Oral mirtazapine 15 mg at night as first-line pharmacotherapy given its sedative properties and appetite stimulation useful in patients with PTSD and comorbid insomnia now
options.rationale: Mirtazapine has limited evidence in PTSD and is a second- or third-line option; SSRIs remain first line based on stronger RCT evidence in this population.

explanation.summary: The RANZCP and NHMRC-endorsed Australian PTSD guidelines recommend an SSRI (sertraline or paroxetine) as first-line pharmacotherapy for PTSD in adults, ideally as an adjunct to trauma-focused psychotherapy. Sertraline is typically started at 50 mg daily and titrated to 100 to 200 mg over 4 to 6 weeks. Benzodiazepines are contraindicated because they impair extinction learning; antipsychotics are augmentation agents only.
key_points: SSRIs (sertraline, paroxetine) are first-line pharmacotherapy for PTSD
Benzodiazepines should be avoided in PTSD
Antipsychotics are augmentation, not first line
Prazosin is specifically for trauma-related nightmares
explanation.pearls: For trauma-related nightmares refractory to SSRI, add prazosin starting at 1 mg at night with blood pressure monitoring; titrate weekly by 1 mg to a maximum of about 15 mg at night.

stem: A 26-year-old woman with known borderline personality disorder presents to your emergency department after superficial cutting to her forearm following an argument with her partner. She has been drinking wine but is coherent. She reports fleeting suicidal thoughts but no current intent or plan. She has attended the emergency department 12 times in the past 6 months for similar presentations. She is currently engaged with a dialectical behaviour therapy program.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 92, BP 118/72, RR 16, SpO2 99 percent, temp 36.7 C
data_table.Examination: Superficial linear lacerations left forearm, no active bleeding, no tendon or nerve involvement, coherent conversation, no gross intoxication
data_table.Investigations: Alcohol breath test 0.06; paracetamol undetectable; ECG normal sinus rhythm

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management plan?

options.text: Admit her as an involuntary patient to a general psychiatric ward under the Mental Health Act for 7 days of containment and to allow safety planning to occur
options.rationale: Involuntary admission for chronic self-harm in BPD is generally counter-therapeutic, reinforcing crisis behaviours and worsening long-term outcomes for the patient over time.

options.text: Administer intramuscular olanzapine 10 mg for behavioural containment and admit for 24 hours of observation to prevent escalation of her presenting complaint tonight
options.rationale: IM olanzapine is not indicated in a coherent cooperative patient without acute agitation, psychosis or mania and would reinforce sedation as a coping strategy long term.

options.text: Wound care and dressing, collaborative safety planning, contact her DBT therapist, then discharge with clear crisis contacts and a written safety plan for home
options.rationale: Best-practice ED management of chronic BPD self-harm is wound care, collaborative safety planning, communication with the treating team and structured discharge; hospital admission is avoided unless acute major mental illness risk is present.

options.text: Commence oral fluoxetine 20 mg daily for chronic suicidality and prescribe a 3 month supply on discharge from the emergency department tonight without further review
options.rationale: There is no strong evidence for SSRIs specifically for chronic self-harm in BPD, and prescribing 3 months of an antidepressant to a patient with chronic suicidality raises overdose risk.

options.text: Refer her to a general medical ward under the medical registrar for observation and then transfer to a psychiatry inpatient bed on the morning ward round tomorrow
options.rationale: Medical admission for uncomplicated superficial cutting is not indicated and delays discharge planning without adding clinical benefit for a patient engaged with DBT.

explanation.summary: Chronic self-harm in borderline personality disorder is best managed in the emergency department by medical wound care, collaborative safety planning with the patient, and communication with the treating DBT team. Discharge is structured with crisis contacts and clear plans for follow-up. Involuntary admission is avoided unless a superimposed acute major mental illness or an escalating atypical presentation raises acute risk. Intramuscular sedation of a cooperative patient reinforces sedation as a coping strategy and is not indicated.
key_points: Involuntary admission for chronic self-harm in BPD is usually counter-therapeutic
ED management: wound care, collaborative safety plan, treating team contact
Sedation for a cooperative patient is not indicated
Limit medication quantities to reduce overdose risk
explanation.pearls: Reserve inpatient admission for BPD when there is superimposed major mental illness, an atypical or escalating pattern, or when brief admission is planned for a specific goal with an agreed discharge date.

stem: A 28-year-old woman with first-episode psychosis has been stable on risperidone 4 mg daily for 8 months. She presents to your clinic complaining of secondary amenorrhoea for 5 months, galactorrhoea and reduced libido. Her serum prolactin is 2800 mIU/L (normal under 500). Pituitary MRI is normal. Beta-hCG is negative. She is otherwise well and has no history of seizures, cardiovascular disease or diabetes. She wants to preserve her current mental state.

data_table.Examination: Alert, cooperative, mood euthymic, no thought disorder, galactorrhoea on breast expression, no visual field defect
data_table.Investigations: Prolactin 2800 mIU/L, MRI pituitary normal, beta-hCG negative, TSH 1.8, LFTs normal, U&E normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Add oral cabergoline 0.25 mg twice weekly to lower the prolactin level over time while continuing her current dose of risperidone 4 mg daily unchanged during this period
options.rationale: Adding a dopamine agonist to an antipsychotic risks triggering relapse of psychosis; the guideline-preferred approach is to switch to a prolactin-sparing antipsychotic rather than add a dopamine agonist.

options.text: Reduce risperidone to 2 mg daily and repeat the prolactin level in 4 weeks to determine whether the level normalises with a lower dose of the current antipsychotic
options.rationale: Prolactin elevation is only weakly dose-related for risperidone at therapeutic doses; halving the dose may destabilise psychosis without normalising the prolactin level in this patient.

options.text: Cease risperidone entirely and commence oral haloperidol 5 mg daily as a first-generation alternative antipsychotic in order to reduce elevated serum prolactin level to normal
options.rationale: Haloperidol raises prolactin at least as much as risperidone; it is not a prolactin-sparing option and would not resolve the endocrine adverse effect she is experiencing.

options.text: Switch antipsychotic to aripiprazole 10 mg daily using a cross-titration schedule over 4 weeks, monitoring closely for relapse of any psychotic symptoms during the switch period
options.rationale: Aripiprazole is prolactin-sparing as a partial dopamine agonist and is the AU-preferred switch strategy for antipsychotic-induced hyperprolactinaemia; olanzapine and quetiapine are also lower-risk options for switching.

options.text: Refer her to endocrinology and continue risperidone at 4 mg daily unchanged while awaiting specialist input over the next 3 to 6 months for further formal assessment
options.rationale: An untreated prolactin above 2000 mIU/L over months increases the risk of bone mineral density loss and persistent amenorrhoea; specific action from psychiatry is needed now.

explanation.summary: Antipsychotic-induced hyperprolactinaemia is most reliably managed by switching to a prolactin-sparing agent. Aripiprazole (partial dopamine agonist) is first choice; olanzapine and quetiapine are lower-risk alternatives compared with risperidone and paliperidone. Cross-titration should be done over 4 weeks with monitoring for symptom recurrence. Adding a dopamine agonist to the current antipsychotic risks psychotic relapse and is generally avoided.
key_points: Switch to aripiprazole is preferred over adding a dopamine agonist
Prolactin elevation is weakly dose-related for risperidone at therapeutic doses
Cross-titrate over 4 weeks and monitor for psychotic relapse
Persistent hyperprolactinaemia risks bone loss and amenorrhoea
explanation.pearls: For patients where a switch is not tolerated, low-dose adjunctive aripiprazole 5 to 10 mg added to the existing antipsychotic has emerging evidence for lowering prolactin without triggering psychosis relapse.

stem: A 30-year-old woman in her first trimester (10 weeks) presents to your general practice with a 6 week history of persistent low mood, anhedonia, poor sleep and thoughts of worthlessness. She has a history of major depressive disorder and has been off medication since planning pregnancy 4 months ago. She has no suicidal intent. She has moderate depression on PHQ-9 (score 16) and has already been referred for perinatal psychology. She wants to consider pharmacotherapy.

data_table.Examination: Alert, tearful at times, cooperative, no psychotic features, no suicidal intent, PHQ-9 16

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first-line antidepressant?

options.text: Oral paroxetine 20 mg daily titrated based on response, then continued throughout pregnancy and into the lactation period with obstetric and mental health team follow-up
options.rationale: Paroxetine is associated with a small increased risk of fetal cardiac malformations (ventricular septal defect) and is generally avoided as a new prescription in pregnancy.

options.text: Oral fluoxetine 20 mg daily titrated based on response, then continued throughout the pregnancy and lactation period with regular obstetric and mental health team monitoring reviews
options.rationale: Fluoxetine is reasonable but has a longer half-life and higher milk-plasma ratio than sertraline; sertraline is preferred as a new prescription in pregnancy for these reasons.

options.text: Oral venlafaxine 75 mg daily titrated based on response, then continued throughout the pregnancy and lactation period with regular obstetric and mental health team monitoring for tolerability
options.rationale: Venlafaxine is associated with increased risk of maternal hypertension and neonatal adaptation syndrome; SSRIs are preferred as first line in pregnancy over SNRIs like venlafaxine.

options.text: Oral mirtazapine 30 mg at night titrated based on response, then continued throughout pregnancy and lactation with regular obstetric and mental health monitoring at each visit
options.rationale: Mirtazapine has a smaller safety database than SSRIs in pregnancy and is not first line; SSRIs remain the preferred first choice for treating depression in the perinatal period.

options.text: Oral sertraline 50 mg daily titrated to therapeutic dose, with obstetric and mental health follow-up throughout pregnancy and continuation planned into the postnatal period
options.rationale: Sertraline is the AU-preferred SSRI for depression in pregnancy due to the largest safety database, minimal placental transfer, and low breast milk concentrations for future breastfeeding.

explanation.summary: For a new prescription in pregnancy, sertraline is the AU-preferred SSRI due to the largest safety database, minimal placental transfer, and lowest breast milk concentrations for future breastfeeding. Paroxetine is avoided in pregnancy because of a small increased risk of fetal cardiac malformations. Fluoxetine and venlafaxine are reasonable if already effective for the woman but are not first-choice new prescriptions.
key_points: Sertraline is first-choice SSRI for a new prescription in pregnancy
Paroxetine avoided due to small VSD risk
Fluoxetine acceptable if already effective, longer half-life
Venlafaxine risks maternal hypertension and neonatal adaptation syndrome
explanation.pearls: Neonatal adaptation syndrome (jitteriness, feeding difficulty, transient tachypnoea) affects 10 to 30 percent of SSRI-exposed neonates; it is short-lived and stopping SSRIs in the third trimester is not recommended because relapse risk exceeds neonatal risk.

subtopic_detail: Serotonin syndrome versus NMS differentiation and treatment
stem: A 42-year-old woman on sertraline 200 mg daily was started on tramadol 50 mg four times daily for back pain 6 hours ago. She now presents to your emergency department with tremor, agitation, diaphoresis and diarrhoea. On examination she has lower limb hyperreflexia and inducible clonus at the ankles, sustained on the right. Muscle tone is normal in the upper limbs. Temperature is 38.9 C. There is no rigidity of the neck or trunk.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 128, BP 158/95, RR 24, SpO2 97 percent, temp 38.9 C
data_table.Examination: Diaphoretic, agitated, dilated pupils, hyperreflexia lower limbs, inducible ankle clonus (sustained right), no lead-pipe rigidity, no dyskinesia
data_table.Investigations: CK 340 U/L, WCC 12, glucose 6.2, U&E normal, ECG sinus tachycardia

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Cease serotonergic agents (sertraline and tramadol), give IV benzodiazepines (diazepam 5 to 10 mg titrated), active external cooling if temperature above 38.5 C, add cyproheptadine 12 mg PO
options.rationale: Serotonin syndrome from a serotonergic combination is treated by ceasing offending agents, benzodiazepines for agitation, active cooling for hyperthermia, and cyproheptadine 12 mg PO stat as an antidote in refractory cases.

options.text: IV dantrolene 2.5 mg/kg push, then cool to 37 C, cease serotonergic agents and admit for benzodiazepine sedation and monitoring in the intensive care unit overnight for stability
options.rationale: Dantrolene is used for NMS or malignant hyperthermia, not serotonin syndrome; the clinical picture here with inducible clonus and diaphoresis 6 hours after adding a serotonergic is serotonin syndrome.

options.text: IV bromocriptine 2.5 mg via nasogastric tube every 8 hours, cease tramadol only, continue sertraline and admit for observation with paracetamol for fever and IV rehydration overnight
options.rationale: Bromocriptine is for NMS, not serotonin syndrome; paracetamol does not treat centrally driven hyperthermia; sertraline must also be ceased as it is the primary serotonergic driver.

options.text: IV haloperidol 5 mg to control agitation, IV normal saline 2 L bolus, continue serotonergic agents to avoid rebound depression and admit for cardiac monitoring and observation overnight
options.rationale: Haloperidol is an antidopaminergic that can precipitate or worsen NMS and dystonia and should be avoided; continuing serotonergic agents in serotonin syndrome is inappropriate.

options.text: IV midazolam 5 mg then intubation with propofol and rocuronium, admit for 48 hours of therapeutic hypothermia to 33 C on the intensive care unit for neuroprotection during recovery
options.rationale: Therapeutic hypothermia to 33 C is used post cardiac arrest, not for serotonin syndrome; simple external cooling to below 38.5 C is sufficient unless the case is refractory.

explanation.summary: Serotonin syndrome presents within hours of a serotonergic combination with the triad of neuromuscular hyperactivity (lower limb hyperreflexia, clonus, tremor), autonomic instability (hyperthermia, tachycardia, mydriasis, diaphoresis, diarrhoea) and altered mental status. It is distinguished from NMS by rapid onset, lower limb dominance, clonus and lower CK. Management is cease serotonergic agents, benzodiazepines, active cooling and cyproheptadine if refractory.
key_points: Serotonin syndrome: clonus, lower limb dominant, autonomic instability, rapid onset
NMS: rigidity, upper motor tone increase, days-long onset, very high CK
Treat serotonin syndrome with benzodiazepines, cooling, cyproheptadine
Avoid haloperidol; it worsens NMS if misdiagnosed
explanation.pearls: Tramadol, linezolid, MAOIs and MDMA are potent serotonergic agents commonly overlooked; a careful drug and supplement history including St John's wort is essential when serotonin syndrome is suspected.

subtopic_detail: Alcohol withdrawal seizure prevention with thiamine dosing
stem: A 48-year-old man is admitted to your surgical ward pre-operatively for elective cholecystectomy tomorrow. He reports drinking 15 standard drinks daily for 20 years. His last drink was 12 hours ago. He is now tremulous, mildly anxious and diaphoretic. He has a CIWA-Ar score of 14. He has no history of seizures. His full blood count and electrolytes are normal but he has a mildly elevated GGT.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 102, BP 152/95, RR 18, SpO2 98 percent, temp 37.1 C
data_table.Examination: Alert, mildly anxious, tremulous, sweaty, no focal neurology, no ataxia or ophthalmoplegia
data_table.Investigations: CIWA-Ar 14, glucose 5.4, U&E normal, LFTs GGT 180 (5 to 55), MCV 102

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial regimen?

options.text: Oral thiamine 100 mg daily plus oral diazepam 5 mg every 6 hours PRN for CIWA-Ar score above 8, and reassess him in the morning ward round before the operating list starts
options.rationale: Oral thiamine 100 mg is inadequate for a high-risk drinker facing surgery; parenteral thiamine at 300 mg IV is preferred to prevent Wernicke encephalopathy in this scenario.

options.text: IV thiamine 300 mg three times daily for at least 3 days before any glucose, oral diazepam symptom-triggered per CIWA-Ar (10 to 20 mg if score above 10), and admit for close monitoring
options.rationale: AU eTG advises IV thiamine 300 mg three times daily for at least 3 to 5 days in high-risk drinkers to prevent Wernicke encephalopathy, plus symptom-triggered oral diazepam guided by CIWA-Ar.

options.text: IV glucose 10 percent at 100 mL per hour, oral diazepam 10 mg every 6 hours fixed dose regimen, IM thiamine 100 mg once daily for 3 days total and observation overnight
options.rationale: Giving glucose before parenteral thiamine can precipitate Wernicke encephalopathy in a chronic heavy drinker; parenteral thiamine must be given first before any glucose infusion.

options.text: Oral chlordiazepoxide 25 mg every 6 hours as fixed-dose reducing regimen without thiamine, and standard nil by mouth from midnight for the elective operation planned tomorrow morning
options.rationale: Withholding thiamine entirely in a chronic heavy drinker risks Wernicke encephalopathy and proceeding to elective surgery risks unmanaged withdrawal intra- and postoperatively; defer surgery.

options.text: IM haloperidol 5 mg for agitation, oral thiamine 100 mg daily, and reduce diazepam to 2 mg every 8 hours PRN in view of the anaesthetic and surgery scheduled for tomorrow morning
options.rationale: Haloperidol lowers seizure threshold and is contraindicated in alcohol withdrawal; benzodiazepines are the definitive treatment for prevention of alcohol withdrawal seizures.

explanation.summary: High-risk alcohol withdrawal (heavy chronic intake, GGT elevated, MCV raised) is managed with parenteral thiamine 300 mg IV three times daily for at least 3 to 5 days to prevent Wernicke encephalopathy, plus symptom-triggered benzodiazepines (oral diazepam) guided by CIWA-Ar. Glucose must not precede thiamine in a chronic heavy drinker. Antipsychotics are contraindicated as they lower seizure threshold, and elective surgery should be deferred until withdrawal is managed.
key_points: IV thiamine 300 mg TDS for at least 3 to 5 days in high-risk drinkers
Thiamine must precede glucose in chronic heavy drinkers
Symptom-triggered diazepam by CIWA-Ar is preferred to fixed-dose
Avoid antipsychotics (lower seizure threshold) and defer elective surgery
explanation.pearls: Wernicke encephalopathy is under-recognised: only 10 percent have the classical triad of ataxia, ophthalmoplegia and confusion at presentation; treat empirically in any at-risk patient with any one of these features.

subtopic_detail: Delirium versus dementia in acute presentation
stem: An 82-year-old woman with mild dementia is brought to your emergency department by her daughter with 2 days of increased confusion, agitation and visual hallucinations of small animals. She has a background of hypertension and a urinary tract infection was treated 3 weeks ago. Cognitive scores have been stable at MMSE 22 for 12 months. On examination her attention is inconsistent, she is disorientated, and she is intermittently drowsy. Physical examination is otherwise unremarkable.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 92, BP 138/84, RR 20, SpO2 96 percent, temp 37.4 C
data_table.Examination: Fluctuating attention (positive months-backwards error), disorientation, drowsy at times, no focal neurology, no meningism
data_table.Investigations: Urinalysis: leucocytes and nitrites positive; U&E, glucose, calcium normal; CXR clear

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Prescribe oral risperidone 2 mg twice daily as a maintenance antipsychotic to control the hallucinations and agitation for at least 4 weeks with a review appointment planned
options.rationale: Antipsychotics for delirium should be short-term, low-dose (risperidone 0.25 to 0.5 mg), reserved for severe distress or safety risk, and reviewed daily; 2 mg twice daily for 4 weeks is inappropriate.

options.text: Refer her for CT head and lumbar puncture to exclude an intracranial cause and CNS infection before starting any treatment for the acute confusional presentation observed today
options.rationale: CT head is warranted if there is focal neurology, recent trauma or anticoagulation, or if no clear precipitant is found; LP if CNS infection is suspected. Neither is a routine first step with a clear UTI.

options.text: Admit for a delirium care package: identify and treat the infection, empirical oral antibiotics, ensure hydration, avoid physical restraints, use environmental de-escalation and family presence
options.rationale: Delirium superimposed on dementia is managed by identifying and treating the precipitant (here likely UTI), maintaining hydration, avoiding restraints, providing quiet single-room care and involving family.

options.text: Cease all her regular antihypertensive medications plus her cholinesterase inhibitor and start IV dexamethasone 8 mg for the acute confusional presentation with agitation observed today
options.rationale: Steroids can worsen delirium and are not indicated. Cholinesterase inhibitors may help dementia symptoms and should not be stopped abruptly during an acute confusional episode.

options.text: Discharge her home with her daughter with education about sundowning and follow up with her general practitioner in one week to reassess her cognitive status and current medications
options.rationale: Discharge home with acute delirium and safety concerns without treating the precipitant is unsafe; admission for management of the delirium and its cause is warranted here today.

explanation.summary: Delirium superimposed on dementia is diagnosed by acute onset, fluctuating attention, altered arousal and disorientation. The precipitant here (likely urinary sepsis) is identified and treated. Non-pharmacological measures are first line: hydration, quiet environment, family involvement, orientation cues, and avoiding restraints. Antipsychotics are last resort at low doses (risperidone 0.25 to 0.5 mg) for severe distress or safety risk.
key_points: Identify and treat the precipitant of delirium (infection, medication, metabolic)
Non-pharmacological measures first line
If antipsychotic needed, low dose (risperidone 0.25 to 0.5 mg), short-term, daily review
CT and LP only if focal signs, trauma, anticoagulation or no clear cause
explanation.pearls: Cholinesterase inhibitors used for dementia do not treat delirium and should not be started acutely for confusion; there is evidence they may worsen delirium duration and outcomes.

stem: A 55-year-old man presents to your regional emergency department with 90 minutes of central crushing chest pain. His ECG shows 3 mm ST elevation in the anterior leads with reciprocal changes. The nearest PCI-capable hospital is 3 hours away by road transport. Air retrieval is not available for at least 2 hours. Troponin has been sent. He has no contraindications to thrombolysis. He weighs 82 kg.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 88, BP 132/82, RR 18, SpO2 98 percent, temp 36.7 C
data_table.Examination: Alert, in pain, no basal crackles, JVP not elevated, no pulmonary oedema, no new murmurs
data_table.Investigations: ECG: 3 mm ST elevation V1 to V4, reciprocal depression II, III, aVF; troponin pending; potassium 4.1; creatinine 90; INR 1.0

lead_in: What is the most appropriate reperfusion strategy?

options.text: Immediate transfer to the PCI centre for primary PCI, targeting a door-to-balloon time of 90 minutes from arrival at the receiving centre for optimal reperfusion outcomes
options.rationale: Transfer for primary PCI is only preferred when total delay to PCI is under 120 minutes from first medical contact; 3 hours by road plus door-to-balloon exceeds this window, so lytics are preferred.

options.text: Wait for the troponin result then start dual antiplatelet therapy and heparin, and admit for medical management without acute reperfusion until further test results are available
options.rationale: STEMI diagnosis is ECG-based; waiting for troponin delays reperfusion. Not offering reperfusion at all is inappropriate for STEMI within 12 hours of symptom onset in a patient without contraindications.

options.text: Intravenous streptokinase 1.5 million units over 60 minutes plus oral aspirin, then defer transfer until pain resolves and further reperfusion needs are reassessed by the retrieval team
options.rationale: Streptokinase is rarely used in Australia due to inferior patency rates and allergy risk; tenecteplase is the preferred fibrinolytic. Transfer should also occur to allow rescue PCI if reperfusion fails.

options.text: Weight-adjusted IV tenecteplase (about 40 mg) plus enoxaparin and clopidogrel now, then transfer for rescue PCI if reperfusion fails or routine early angiography 3 to 24 hours
options.rationale: When primary PCI cannot be delivered within 120 minutes of first medical contact, prehospital or in-hospital fibrinolysis with weight-adjusted tenecteplase is preferred, followed by early transfer for pharmacoinvasive PCI.

options.text: IV nitroglycerin infusion titrated to pain relief, oral aspirin and metoprolol, and admit locally for medical management until pain resolves and the troponin trajectory becomes clearer over time
options.rationale: Nitrates and beta-blockers do not reperfuse the coronary artery; reperfusion is the priority in STEMI within 12 hours of symptom onset in a patient without contraindications to thrombolysis.

explanation.summary: In STEMI, primary PCI is preferred when it can be delivered within 120 minutes of first medical contact. Beyond this window, weight-adjusted bolus tenecteplase (with enoxaparin and clopidogrel or ticagrelor as per local protocol) is given without delay, followed by early transfer to a PCI centre for rescue PCI if reperfusion fails or routine coronary angiography at 3 to 24 hours (pharmacoinvasive strategy). Waiting for troponin or omitting reperfusion is inappropriate.
key_points: Primary PCI preferred if within 120 min of first medical contact
Otherwise fibrinolysis with tenecteplase then transfer
Rescue PCI if failed reperfusion; routine angiography 3 to 24 hours
STEMI diagnosis is ECG-based; do not wait for troponin
explanation.pearls: Failed reperfusion after fibrinolysis is defined as under 50 percent ST resolution at 60 to 90 minutes, ongoing chest pain, or haemodynamic instability; these mandate immediate rescue PCI, not repeat lytics.

stem: A 65-year-old man presents to your emergency department with 3 days of productive cough, right-sided pleuritic chest pain and fever. He has a background of well-controlled type 2 diabetes. On examination he has right lower zone crackles and bronchial breathing. Chest x-ray shows a dense right lower lobe consolidation. Confusion Assessment Method is negative. His CURB-65 score is 1 (age 65 or over, plus one additional point).

data_table.Vital signs: HR 102, BP 128/78, RR 26, SpO2 91 percent room air, temp 38.6 C
data_table.Examination: Alert, orientated, right lower zone crackles and bronchial breathing, no signs of shock
data_table.Investigations: Urea 6.2 mmol/L, WCC 18, CRP 240, sodium 138, creatinine 90; CXR right lower lobe consolidation

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial antibiotic strategy?

options.text: Oral amoxicillin 1 g three times daily plus oral doxycycline 100 mg twice daily for 5 days, home management with a general practitioner review at 48 hours to reassess
options.rationale: Home management may be acceptable for very low severity (CURB-65 0 to 1 with no adverse features) but hypoxia at SpO2 91 percent and RR 26 are adverse features so hospital IV therapy is preferred.

options.text: IV piperacillin-tazobactam 4.5 g every 8 hours plus IV azithromycin 500 mg once daily for 7 days total, targeting broad spectrum cover for the community-acquired pneumonia observed today
options.rationale: Broad spectrum cover with anti-pseudomonal beta-lactam is reserved for severe pneumonia or specific risk factors (structural lung disease, healthcare exposure) and is not first line for moderate CAP.

options.text: IV ceftriaxone 2 g once daily plus IV vancomycin 15 mg/kg twice daily for 10 days, providing empirical MRSA cover for the community-acquired pneumonia observed today at admission
options.rationale: Vancomycin is added only when there is necrotising pneumonia, cavitation or specific MRSA risk factors; empirical addition for community-acquired pneumonia is inappropriate as first-line therapy.

options.text: Oral moxifloxacin 400 mg once daily for 5 days plus oseltamivir 75 mg twice daily for 5 days, then discharge home to community with a general practitioner follow-up appointment in 2 days
options.rationale: Moxifloxacin monotherapy for CAP has QT and mycobacterial concerns; oseltamivir requires evidence of influenza; home management with hypoxia at SpO2 91 percent is not safe management.

options.text: IV benzylpenicillin 1.2 g every 6 hours plus oral doxycycline 100 mg twice daily for 7 days total, then switch to oral therapy once he is clinically stable and improving
options.rationale: AU eTG for moderate-severity community-acquired pneumonia requiring hospitalisation is IV benzylpenicillin plus oral doxycycline, switching to oral therapy once clinically stable, tolerating oral, and improving inflammatory markers.

explanation.summary: Moderate-severity community-acquired pneumonia requiring hospital admission is treated in Australia with IV benzylpenicillin 1.2 g every 6 hours plus oral doxycycline 100 mg twice daily to cover atypicals. Once the patient is clinically stable (afebrile 24 hours, tolerating oral, improving inflammatory markers, no hypoxia), switch to oral amoxicillin 1 g TDS plus doxycycline for a total 7 day course. Broad-spectrum agents are reserved for severe disease or specific risk factors.
key_points: Moderate CAP: IV benzylpenicillin plus oral doxycycline
Switch to oral when clinically stable; total 7 days
CURB-65 useful for severity but adverse features (hypoxia, RR) also decide admission
Broad-spectrum only for severe disease or specific risk factors
explanation.pearls: IV to oral switch is safe when the patient has stable vitals for 24 hours, is tolerating oral, is haemodynamically stable, has improving CRP and WCC, and there is no pleural infection; do not wait for the CXR to clear.

subtopic_detail: Warfarin peri-procedural bridging for elective surgery
stem: A 68-year-old woman with atrial fibrillation (CHA2DS2-VASc score 4) is on warfarin with INR 2.5. She is scheduled for an elective knee arthroplasty in 7 days. She has no history of prior stroke or systemic embolism, no mechanical heart valve, and no recent (under 3 months) venous thromboembolism. She has moderate renal impairment with eGFR 45. There has been no recent bleeding.

data_table.Examination: Alert, well, ECG atrial fibrillation, no signs of embolism or bleeding
data_table.Investigations: INR 2.5, Hb 128, platelets 260, creatinine 105, eGFR 45

lead_in: What is the most appropriate peri-procedural anticoagulation plan?

options.text: Stop warfarin 5 days before surgery, no bridging heparin required, then restart warfarin 12 to 24 hours after surgery when adequate haemostasis has been achieved by the surgical team
options.rationale: For atrial fibrillation without mechanical valve, prior stroke or recent VTE, BRIDGE trial evidence shows no bridging is preferred; bridging LMWH increases bleeding without reducing stroke.

options.text: Continue warfarin at usual dose throughout the perioperative period since the bleeding risk of primary knee arthroplasty is generally acceptably low in most patients undergoing the procedure
options.rationale: Elective knee arthroplasty is a high bleeding risk procedure; warfarin must be held perioperatively to avoid intra- and postoperative bleeding requiring transfusion and reoperation.

options.text: Stop warfarin 5 days before surgery and bridge with therapeutic-dose enoxaparin 1 mg/kg twice daily starting 3 days before the operation and continuing until the day of surgery this year
options.rationale: Full-dose bridging is reserved for very high thromboembolic risk (mechanical mitral valve, recent stroke or VTE under 3 months, CHA2DS2-VASc 7 or more); this patient does not meet those criteria.

options.text: Stop warfarin 3 days before surgery and give oral vitamin K 5 mg to accelerate INR normalisation before the procedure and cross-match blood for the operation planned to occur this week
options.rationale: Routine oral vitamin K creates warfarin resistance postoperatively, delaying re-anticoagulation; 5 days off warfarin without vitamin K reliably normalises the INR in most patients.

options.text: Switch warfarin to apixaban 5 mg twice daily starting 5 days before surgery, then hold apixaban 24 hours before the surgery scheduled for later next week and restart afterwards on advice
options.rationale: Switching between anticoagulants perioperatively adds complexity and cost without benefit, introducing a gap or overlap; simple hold of warfarin is the standard perioperative strategy.

explanation.summary: For atrial fibrillation on warfarin without mechanical valve, recent stroke, recent VTE, or CHA2DS2-VASc of 7 or more, the BRIDGE trial showed no benefit to LMWH bridging and increased bleeding risk. Stop warfarin 5 days before surgery, do not bridge, and restart warfarin 12 to 24 hours after surgery when haemostasis is achieved. Vitamin K acceleration causes postoperative warfarin resistance and should be avoided routinely.
key_points: No bridging for AF unless mechanical valve, recent stroke, recent VTE or CHA2DS2-VASc 7+
Stop warfarin 5 days pre-op
Restart warfarin 12 to 24 hours post-op when haemostasis achieved
Routine oral vitamin K causes postoperative warfarin resistance
explanation.pearls: Full-dose bridging LMWH is contraindicated within 24 hours of major surgery and is generally started 3 days before and stopped 24 hours before; prophylactic-dose LMWH can be used postoperatively for surgical VTE prophylaxis.

stem: A 74-year-old woman with newly diagnosed small cell lung cancer presents to your medical assessment unit with 5 days of nausea, unsteadiness and mild headache. She is on no diuretics. Her serum sodium is 118 mmol/L (baseline 138 two weeks ago), plasma osmolality 254 mOsm/kg, urine osmolality 480 mOsm/kg, urine sodium 55 mmol/L. She is euvolaemic clinically. TSH and cortisol are normal. She is alert with no focal neurology.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 78, BP 128/78 lying, 124/76 standing, RR 16, SpO2 97 percent, temp 36.7 C
data_table.Examination: Alert, orientated, no ataxia, no focal neurology, mucous membranes moist, JVP visible at 4 cm, no oedema
data_table.Investigations: Na 118, K 4.0, urea 3.4, creatinine 60, plasma osm 254, urine osm 480, urine Na 55, TSH 1.8, cortisol 480

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial management?

options.text: Infuse 1 litre of 0.9 percent normal saline over 4 hours and reassess her sodium level after each litre until the serum sodium level reaches 130 mmol/L or above
options.rationale: Isotonic saline in SIADH can paradoxically worsen hyponatraemia because urine osmolality (480) exceeds infused osmolality; water is retained while sodium is excreted in the urine.
source_refs: European Society of Endocrinology hyponatraemia guideline

options.text: Restrict fluids to 800 mL/day with sodium and neurological monitoring twice daily, aiming to raise serum sodium by no more than 8 mmol/L per 24 hours to avoid osmotic demyelination
options.rationale: Euvolaemic hyponatraemia with concentrated urine and euvolaemia meets SIADH criteria; first-line management is fluid restriction (800 to 1000 mL/day) with monitoring and limiting correction to under 8 mmol/L per 24 hours.
source_refs: European Society of Endocrinology hyponatraemia guideline

options.text: Give 3 percent hypertonic saline 150 mL bolus over 20 minutes to rapidly correct the serum sodium above 125 mmol/L within the next 4 hours, aiming to abolish symptoms quickly today
options.rationale: Hypertonic saline is reserved for severe symptomatic hyponatraemia (seizures, coma, severe drowsiness); this patient has only mild symptoms and can be managed with fluid restriction first.
source_refs: European Society of Endocrinology hyponatraemia guideline

options.text: Prescribe oral demeclocycline 300 mg four times daily and continue an unrestricted oral fluid intake for maintenance, with monitoring of the serum sodium level daily on the ward round
options.rationale: Demeclocycline is now rarely used due to nephrotoxicity and slow onset; tolvaptan is preferred if pharmacotherapy is needed after fluid restriction has failed to produce an adequate response.
source_refs: European Society of Endocrinology hyponatraemia guideline

options.text: Give IV furosemide 40 mg with oral salt tablets, then correct the serum sodium with a 2 percent saline infusion titrated overnight to rise no more than 8 mmol/L in the first 24 hours
options.rationale: Furosemide plus salt tablets is a niche second-line strategy in SIADH; not first line and carries a risk of overcorrection and electrolyte disturbance without benefit over fluid restriction.
source_refs: European Society of Endocrinology hyponatraemia guideline

explanation.summary: SIADH diagnostic criteria are met with euvolaemic hypotonic hyponatraemia (plasma osm below 275), inappropriately concentrated urine (urine osm above 100), and urine sodium above 30 mmol/L, with normal thyroid and adrenal function, no diuretic use and no volume depletion. First-line management is fluid restriction 800 to 1000 mL/day; hypertonic saline is reserved for severe symptomatic disease. Correction is limited to under 8 mmol/L per 24 hours to prevent osmotic demyelination.
key_points: SIADH: euvolaemic, plasma osm low, urine osm > 100, urine Na > 30, normal TFTs and cortisol
First line: fluid restrict 800 to 1000 mL/day
Isotonic saline can paradoxically worsen SIADH
Correct no more than 8 mmol/L in 24 hours; hypertonic saline only for severe symptoms
explanation.pearls: If overcorrection occurs (sodium rises more than 8 mmol/L in 24 hours), stop all sodium sources, administer 5 percent dextrose IV, and consider desmopressin 2 microgram IV to prevent osmotic demyelination.

sources.label: European Society of Endocrinology hyponatraemia guideline

subtopic_detail: HHS versus DKA insulin infusion approach
stem: A 76-year-old man with type 2 diabetes on metformin and gliclazide presents to your emergency department after 5 days of polyuria and progressive drowsiness following a chest infection. His glucose is 42 mmol/L, sodium 152, potassium 4.0, urea 18, creatinine 130. Venous gas pH 7.34, bicarbonate 20, blood ketones 0.4 mmol/L. Calculated effective osmolality is 336 mOsm/kg. He is drowsy but rousable, significantly dehydrated with dry mucous membranes and reduced skin turgor.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 118, BP 100/60, RR 22, SpO2 96 percent, temp 37.6 C, weight 80 kg
data_table.Examination: Drowsy, GCS 13, dry mucous membranes, reduced skin turgor, capillary refill 3 seconds, no focal neurology, chest crepitations right base
data_table.Investigations: Glucose 42, Na 152, K 4.0, urea 18, creatinine 130, VBG pH 7.34, HCO3 20, ketones 0.4, effective osm 336

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial fluid and insulin approach?

options.text: IV 0.9 percent saline 1 litre over 1 hour, then continue at 250 mL/hour and commence IV insulin infusion at 0.05 units/kg/hour immediately once serum potassium is above 3.5 mmol/L
options.rationale: HHS: give fluid first (1 L over 1 hour, reassess), start insulin low-dose 0.05 units/kg/hour and only after several hours when glucose ceases falling with fluids; rapid insulin causes cerebral oedema.
source_refs: JBDS-IP: Management of hyperosmolar hyperglycaemic state

options.text: IV 0.9 percent saline 2 litres over 1 hour, commence IV insulin infusion at 0.1 units/kg/hour immediately upon admission and aim for a glucose fall of 10 mmol/L per hour with observation
options.rationale: 0.1 units/kg/hour is the DKA regimen; in HHS this rate causes too-rapid osmotic shifts leading to cerebral oedema and cardiovascular collapse. Target glucose fall in HHS is 5 mmol/L per hour.
source_refs: JBDS-IP: Management of hyperosmolar hyperglycaemic state

options.text: IV 0.9 percent saline 1 litre over 1 hour, reassess volume status, then only add low-dose insulin at 0.05 units/kg/hour if glucose fails to fall by 5 mmol/L per hour with fluids alone
options.rationale: AU HHS management: aggressive but careful isotonic fluid is primary; insulin is low-dose (0.05 units/kg/hour) and delayed, only added when glucose stops falling with fluids alone, targeting 5 mmol/L fall per hour.
source_refs: JBDS-IP: Management of hyperosmolar hyperglycaemic state

options.text: IV 5 percent dextrose 1 litre over 2 hours, then an IV insulin bolus of 10 units followed by a 0.1 units/kg/hour infusion, targeting a glucose of 8 mmol/L within the next 4 hours today
options.rationale: 5 percent dextrose worsens hyperglycaemia; insulin bolus is not recommended in DKA or HHS; targeting 8 mmol/L within 4 hours is far too rapid an osmolar correction for HHS management.
source_refs: JBDS-IP: Management of hyperosmolar hyperglycaemic state

options.text: IV Hartmann's 500 mL over 1 hour, commence subcutaneous insulin glargine 20 units at bedtime, treat chest infection and reassess him again in the morning on the ward round after handover
options.rationale: Subcutaneous long-acting insulin has slow onset and cannot be titrated in an acutely unwell patient; IV insulin infusion (once fluid-resuscitated and if needed) is required for HHS.
source_refs: JBDS-IP: Management of hyperosmolar hyperglycaemic state

explanation.summary: HHS differs from DKA in that acidosis and significant ketosis are absent, and effective osmolality is markedly raised (over 320 mOsm/kg). Management prioritises IV fluid resuscitation with 0.9 percent saline (1 L in the first hour then reassess), which alone usually reduces glucose by 5 mmol/L per hour. Insulin is started at low dose (0.05 units/kg/hour) and delayed until glucose ceases falling with fluids. Target correction is 5 mmol/L per hour fall.
key_points: HHS: acidosis absent, ketones minimal, effective osmolality > 320
Fluid resuscitation is primary; insulin low-dose and delayed
Target glucose fall 5 mmol/L per hour, not 10
Rapid osmolar correction causes cerebral oedema and haemodynamic collapse
explanation.pearls: HHS has a mortality of 15 to 20 percent compared with 1 to 5 percent for DKA; identifying and treating the precipitant (commonly infection, myocardial infarction, medication non-adherence) is crucial.
