stem: A 72-year-old man with type 2 diabetes and stage 3B chronic kidney disease (eGFR 38) is booked for a CT coronary angiogram tomorrow. His usual medications are metformin, ramipril, spironolactone, atorvastatin and gliclazide. He has recently increased his frusemide because of ankle swelling. His serum creatinine has been stable and his blood pressure is well controlled. He has no history of allergy to contrast media.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 74, BP 132/80, RR 16, weight 84 kg
data_table.Examination: Alert, mild pitting ankle oedema, chest clear, JVP not raised
data_table.Investigations: Creatinine 155, eGFR 38, K 4.4, Hb 128, HbA1c 7.2 percent, BNP 240

lead_in: What is the most appropriate contrast nephropathy prevention plan?

options.text: Give IV N-acetylcysteine 1200 mg twice daily for 24 hours pre-procedure and 24 hours post-procedure, and continue all of his usual medications through the procedure without dose changes
options.rationale: Recent evidence (PRESERVE trial) shows no benefit of N-acetylcysteine over placebo for contrast-induced nephropathy prevention; it is no longer recommended in contemporary practice guidelines.

options.text: Continue metformin and diuretics but withhold ramipril for 48 hours before the procedure, and no IV hydration is required for a patient with an eGFR greater than 30 mL/min/1.73m2 undergoing contrast
options.rationale: Metformin should be temporarily held from the day of contrast when eGFR is under 60 until renal function is confirmed stable 48 hours later, due to lactic acidosis risk; ACEi and diuretics are also usually held.

options.text: Prescribe oral sodium bicarbonate 3 g twice daily for 3 days before and 3 days after the procedure without other measures for prevention of contrast-induced nephropathy in this high-risk patient today
options.rationale: Sodium bicarbonate is non-superior to isotonic saline for CIN prevention (PRESERVE); IV isotonic saline hydration is the standard first-line prophylaxis in patients with additional risk factors like diabetes.

options.text: Withhold metformin, spironolactone, ramipril and frusemide from the day of procedure, IV 0.9 percent saline at 1 mL/kg/hour for 12 hours before and 12 hours after, use lowest effective iso-osmolar contrast
options.rationale: AU KHA-CARI approach for eGFR 30 to 45 with additional risk factors (diabetes, HF, ACEi, diuretics): withhold nephrotoxic and metformin drugs, provide 12-hour peri-procedural isotonic saline hydration, minimise contrast volume with iso-osmolar agent.

options.text: Cancel the CT coronary angiogram and proceed to invasive coronary angiography with a stress cardiac MRI to avoid all contrast exposure for the patient in view of his renal impairment and comorbidities
options.rationale: Invasive coronary angiography uses more contrast than CT; MRI does not replace anatomical coronary imaging. Preventive strategies allow the CT to proceed safely in most patients at risk.

explanation.summary: Contrast-induced nephropathy prevention in high-risk patients (eGFR under 45, diabetes, heart failure, ACEi/ARB/diuretics/NSAIDs) requires withholding nephrotoxic medications and temporary cessation of metformin because of lactic acidosis risk. IV isotonic saline at 1 mL/kg/hour is given for 12 hours before and 12 hours after the procedure. The lowest effective iso-osmolar or low-osmolar contrast volume should be used. N-acetylcysteine and sodium bicarbonate are not superior to saline hydration (PRESERVE trial 2018) and are no longer recommended.
key_points: Withhold metformin (day of contrast); recheck creatinine at 48 hours before resuming
Withhold ACEi/ARB/diuretics peri-procedure in high-risk patients
IV isotonic saline 1 mL/kg/hour 12 hours pre and post
Use lowest effective iso-osmolar contrast volume
explanation.pearls: Post-contrast acute kidney injury is now considered rarer than previously for IV studies, but the highest-risk group remains diabetics with eGFR under 30 or acute kidney injury; radiologist and cardiologist should be informed to minimise volume.

subtopic_detail: Empirical antibiotics in urosepsis with recent ESBL history
stem: A 78-year-old woman is transferred from her nursing home to your emergency department with 24 hours of confusion, fever and hypotension. She is known to have recurrent urinary tract infections and has had two admissions for ESBL Escherichia coli urosepsis in the past 6 months. On examination she is drowsy, hypotensive despite 2 litres of IV fluids, and has suprapubic tenderness. Bloods show creatinine 220 (baseline 90), lactate 3.6 and CRP 320. She is not pregnant.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 118, BP 88/54 (post 2 L fluids), RR 26, SpO2 96 percent, temp 39.1 C
data_table.Examination: Drowsy, GCS 13, warm peripheries, capillary refill 3 seconds, suprapubic tenderness, no flank pain
data_table.Investigations: Creatinine 220 (baseline 90), urea 14, lactate 3.6, WCC 22, CRP 320, urinalysis leucocytes and nitrites positive

lead_in: What is the most appropriate empirical antibiotic and dosing decision?

options.text: IV amoxicillin 2 g every 6 hours plus IV gentamicin 5 mg/kg once daily until cultures return with sensitivities, with standard renal dose adjustment being applied for gentamicin in her acute kidney injury
options.rationale: Amoxicillin plus gentamicin does not reliably cover ESBL organisms; empirical cover for a patient with recent ESBL infection and septic shock must include a carbapenem for adequate empirical activity.

options.text: IV ceftriaxone 2 g once daily as empirical monotherapy, then add ampicillin only if enterococcal cover is judged required by microbiology, and continue ward-based care with hourly BP monitoring overnight
options.rationale: Ceftriaxone will not cover ESBL organisms which produce enzymes that hydrolyse third-generation cephalosporins; ward-based care is inappropriate for septic shock unresponsive to initial 2 L fluids.

options.text: IV piperacillin-tazobactam 4.5 g every 8 hours dose-reduced for the acute kidney injury, and continue ward-based care with hourly blood pressure monitoring and delayed reassessment in the morning ward round
options.rationale: Piperacillin-tazobactam has poor reliability in ESBL bacteraemia (MERINO trial showed higher mortality vs meropenem); ICU-level care is required for shock unresponsive to fluid resuscitation.

options.text: IV vancomycin 25 mg/kg loading then 15 mg/kg every 12 hours, plus IV metronidazole 500 mg every 8 hours for anaerobic cover, and admit her under general medicine for ongoing care and daily specialist review
options.rationale: Vancomycin plus metronidazole covers gram-positive and anaerobic infection but does not cover ESBL gram-negative pathogens driving her urosepsis, and misses the causative organism entirely today.

options.text: IV meropenem 1 g every 8 hours dose-adjusted for creatinine clearance, obtain blood and urine cultures before the first dose, and escalate to ICU for haemodynamic support and vasopressors
options.rationale: For septic shock with recent history of ESBL urosepsis, empirical carbapenem cover (meropenem) is appropriate and dose-adjusted; cultures should be taken before antibiotics if this does not delay administration beyond 45 minutes.

explanation.summary: In septic shock with a history of ESBL infection in the past 6 months, empirical antibiotic cover should include a carbapenem (meropenem 1 g every 8 hours, dose-adjusted for creatinine clearance). Piperacillin-tazobactam is inferior to meropenem for ESBL bacteraemia (MERINO trial 2018). Blood and urine cultures should be obtained before antibiotics only if this does not delay administration beyond 45 minutes. Septic shock unresponsive to 2 L of fluid warrants ICU-level care and vasopressor consideration.
key_points: ESBL history in the past 6 months: cover empirically with a carbapenem
Piperacillin-tazobactam inferior to meropenem for ESBL bacteraemia (MERINO)
Cultures before antibiotics only if no delay beyond 45 minutes
Septic shock unresponsive to 2 L fluid: escalate to ICU and vasopressors
explanation.pearls: For a patient with ESBL history but who is haemodynamically stable and not septic, oral fosfomycin 3 g single dose or oral pivmecillinam are options for uncomplicated ESBL cystitis, sparing carbapenems.

sources.label: MERINO trial: piperacillin-tazobactam vs meropenem for ESBL
